Workload-Static Optical Circuit Switching for Scalable LLM Inference Decode

 

Maximilian Thürmer 1  Nicolas Scotto di Perto 1  Eloise Stein 1  Natanijel Vasic 1  Mikaeil Bagherli 1  Zhenguo Wu 2  Benjamin Klenk 2  Holger Fröning 3  Johannes Feldmann 1 

††footnotetext: 1Salience Labs Ltd, 100 Park Drive, Oxfordshire, OX14 4RY, United Kingdom 2NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara, CA, USA 3Hardware and Artificial Intelligence Lab, Heidelberg University, Germany. Correspondence to: Maximilian Thürmer <max@saliencelabs.ai>.
Abstract

LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with gxnet, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65 % and energy efficiency by up to 119 % over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

1 Introduction

Large language model inference increasingly stresses not only accelerator throughput, but also latency, energy efficiency, and system cost. While training and prefill are dominated by large matrix operations and comparatively large communication transfers, autoregressive decode generates one token or verifies only a few at a time and repeatedly executes fine-grained communication whose latency directly affects user-facing responsiveness Yu et al. (2022); Kwon et al. (2023); Zhong et al. (2024); Agrawal et al. (2024b).

At the same time, growing model size, mixture-of-experts architectures, and long-context inference increase parameter, activation, and KV-cache footprints Kwon et al. (2023); Aminabadi et al. (2022); DeepSeek-AI and others (2026). As these requirements outgrow per-accelerator memory capacity, individual model instances increasingly span many accelerators Aminabadi et al. (2022); Bhatia et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025), creating pressure to extend tightly coupled scale-up fabrics to larger domains and beyond conventional rack boundaries Shou et al. (2025); Zuo and others (2025); Bhargava et al. (2026).

The consequence is a tension between scale and latency: decode benefits from low token-to-token latency and therefore low round-trip time within the scale-up fabric Singhania et al. (2026). However, extending electronic-packet-switched scale-up networks beyond a single rack typically requires additional switching levels, longer physical paths, or both, increasing end-to-end communication latency.

Optical links are attractive for spanning larger accelerator domains, while optical circuit switching (OCS) can avoid repeated electronic packet switching (EPS) at intermediate levels Jouppi et al. (2023). Figure 1 contrasts conventional packet-switched fabrics with our workload-static OCS approach: circuits are configured for the model deployment and reused throughout decode rather than reconfigured within the token-generation loop. Efficient use of such circuits requires physical topology, routing, collective schedules, device placement, and model parallelization to be co-designed Wang et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2024); Jouppi et al. (2023).

Prior work has addressed distributed training Narayanan et al. (2021); Jiang et al. (2024), workload and network simulation Won et al. (2023); Agrawal et al. (2024a), inference serving and disaggregation Yu et al. (2022); Kwon et al. (2023); Agrawal et al. (2024b); Zhong et al. (2024); Patel et al. (2024); Qin et al. (2025), and expert- or context-parallel inference DeepSeek-AI and others (2024); Zhu et al. (2025); Zuo and others (2025); Yang et al. (2025); Bhatia et al. (2025). These approaches improve accelerator utilization and throughput, but do not remove the latency sensitivity of low-batch or high-interactivity11 1 We use interactivity to denote the per-user token generation rate, i.e., tokens per second per active user, the inverse of token-to-token latency during autoregressive decode. decode.

OCS has been explored for datacenter networks Poutievski et al. (2022); Liu et al. (2023), scale-out fabrics Wang et al. (2023), and distributed training Jouppi et al. (2023); Khani et al. (2021); Liao et al. (2025); Shou et al. (2025), typically for provisioning, topology optimization, or workload-phase-dependent reconfiguration. Decode poses a different challenge: communication occurs at fine temporal granularity, while OCS reconfiguration is generally too slow to follow the token-generation loop. This makes per-token optical reconfiguration unattractive for latency-critical inference.

The co-design of decode parallelization, collective communication, and optical scale-up topology remains underexplored. For inference decode, the central question is not whether OCS can follow token-level communication changes dynamically, but whether the communication pattern can be regularized and scheduled such that an optical topology can be configured once and reused throughout serving.

This work studies workload-static OCS as a scale-up network design point for large-scale LLM inference decode. The OCS fabric is configured at deployment time and kept fixed during token generation, acting as a workload-specific static optical topology that realizes the logical communication structure of distributed decode. For a fixed model, context regime, accelerator allocation, service-level objective (interactivity target) and parallelization strategy, communication patterns are known at deployment time. Even in mixture-of-experts inference, token routing only modulates volume, not connectivity: production all-to-all kernels communicate with every peer of a fixed expert-parallel group during each call, with statically allocated per-peer buffers, and with batches padded to pre-captured accelerator execution graph sizes NVIDIA (2026g); vLLM Project (2026b).

Evaluating distributed AI workloads on compute systems requires exploring model architectures, parallelization strategies, accelerator properties, collective algorithms, and network topologies that are difficult to benchmark directly at full scale. Physical access to hundreds of future-generation accelerators is limited, and production traces are tied to specific hardware and software stacks. A flexible modeling framework is therefore needed to study the design space while grounding assumptions in kernel and communication behavior measured on real hardware.

This work makes the following contributions.

  1. 1.

    We introduce workload-static OCS for LLM inference decode: optical circuits are configured once per deployment and co-designed with model parallelization and topology-aware collective schedules to realize recurring communication demand with low-latency logical overlays.

  2. 2.

    We introduce gxnet, a graph-based distributed LLM workload emulation framework that transforms model-level computation graphs into distributed execution traces with explicit compute, memory, and communication operators.

  3. 3.

    We combine analytical and event-based network modeling for all-EPS, hybrid EPS/OCS, and all-OCS scale-up fabrics. The analytical model supports broad design-space exploration, while a flit-level simulator estimates collective execution time, routing behavior, credit effects, and link utilization.

  4. 4.

    We evaluate 1T- and 5T-parameter MoE decode across 128–512 serving accelerators in a 576-accelerator scale-up domain. All-OCS improves interactivity by up to 65 % and system-level energy efficiency by up to 119 % over all-EPS, while sensitivity analysis over bandwidth, radix, and accelerator latency identifies the regimes in which workload-static OCS is most beneficial.

More broadly, we argue that inference specialization should extend beyond accelerators to the scale-up network: communication structure known before execution need not be rediscovered dynamically by a general-purpose packet fabric.

2 Background and Related Work

There is a large corpus of prior literature which addresses many separate pieces of the work presented here. Some work is devoted to related use cases - e.g. training rather than inference. Other contributions focus on a subset of the design space addressed here - for instance ignoring the co-optimization of collective schedules and underlying network topology:

Large scale distributed LLM training has received wide attention in the past. The parallelization strategies were studied Narayanan et al. (2021) and cast into analytical, roofline-based models Isaev et al. (2023). Other approaches which seek to model computation and communication separately are partially based on real hardware traces or synthetic ones that are then feeding a network simulator Won et al. (2023). These approaches, however, have been developed for training. Calculon Isaev et al. (2023) models the scale-up and scale-out networks with single-level latency and bandwidth parameters and assumes bandwidth-optimal collective implementations, which captures step time for large, bandwidth-dominated collectives but not the small, latency-bound collectives of decode. Network simulators such as ASTRA-sim Won et al. (2023) resolve communication in more detail, but do not treat parallelization strategy, collective schedule, and optical circuit topology as a joint design space. Inference-specific simulators such as Vidur Agrawal et al. (2024a) and LLMServingSim Cho et al. (2024) address serving-level questions such as scheduling, batching, and deployment configuration; their communication model is either profiled on existing hardware Agrawal et al. (2024a) or inherited from ASTRA-sim Cho et al. (2024), so the scale-up fabric is not a design variable.

Inference serving and disaggregation methods have been widely described Yu et al. (2022); Kwon et al. (2023); NVIDIA (2026g); Zhong et al. (2024); Patel et al. (2024); Qin et al. (2025). In particular, advances in prefill/decode disaggregation Zhong et al. (2024); Patel et al. (2024) have identified the difference in computation, memory access and network access footprints between prefill and decode phases as a root cause of inefficient inference serving. Consequently, recent work explores dedicated hardware for these two phases of inference and extends this approach by further decomposing the decode phase into attention and feed-forward-network portions, resulting in heterogeneous inference hardware NVIDIA (2026b); Zhu et al. (2025), while others argue that shifting phase ratios favor a single balanced accelerator Ho et al. (2026). In these cases, the network architectures remain packet-switched Ho et al. (2026); Microsoft (2026) or use fixed direct-connect topologies Bhargava et al. (2026); Google (2026) whose physical connectivity is not tailored to the workload, with many accelerator links reaching into the scale-up network.

Extensive work has examined the role of OCS in AI compute clusters ever since the inception of Google’s TPUv4 Jouppi et al. (2023). There has been work focusing on optimizing the network topology through OCS Wang et al. (2023); Liao et al. (2025) and investigations into the required reconfiguration speeds of OCS control planes and optical transceiver relock times to exploit the very predictable and long-running nature of large collective operations resulting from AI training workloads such that an OCS operates more like an optical burst switch (OBS) Wu et al. (2025). Harvest Rahman et al. (2026) and its precursors Hammer et al. (2025); Addanki (2025) go further and synthesize optimal circuit schedules within individual collectives of scale-up domains, which requires fast OCS reconfiguration and tight coupling of the OCS and accelerator control planes, advancing the OCS towards something close to an optical packet switch. Other work has tried to leverage the dual network approach, scale-up inside the rack/box, scale-out between them - to reshape scale-out traffic within the scale-up domain such that the scale-out fabric reduces to rails Wang et al. (2024) that can in turn be realized with OCS Ding et al. (2025). Apart from Harvest, all this work addresses training use cases and focuses on collective schedules for bandwidth optimality as a natural consequence.

In latency-sensitive decode, bandwidth-optimal collective schedules are not necessarily latency-optimal, and resulting collective schedules on scale-up networks are already showing an increasing specialization by expected traffic volume as a consequence NVIDIA (2026e). In decode, tensor, KV-cache, and expert parallelism can induce frequent collectives with small payloads, exposing accelerator-to-accelerator round-trip time rather than only aggregate bandwidth. Optimized communication kernels based on remote-store operations reduce software overhead, but not the underlying sensitivity to fabric latency. In parallel, collective acceleration engines Google (2026); Meta (2026) are moving collective execution into dedicated accelerator hardware. Serving stacks already select collective implementations, but through fixed, offline-tuned heuristics NVIDIA (2026e). Exposing communication explicitly to an automated mapping and scheduling search is a step towards co-optimizing serving and collective implementation Ho et al. (2026), but the repercussions on the ideal network fabric serving the chosen collectives, or even network topology co-optimization for the chosen collective, remain open. The work presented here exploits this specialization more systematically by extending it from the collective schedule to the scale-up topology. It extends the idea of short-circuiting ring collectives Hammer et al. (2025) but, in contrast to per-collective reconfiguration Rahman et al. (2026), derives one topology for the composite decode schedule, i.e., for all collectives of inference decode at once, which the OCS then holds throughout serving, removing reconfiguration from the decode critical path.

3 Workload-Static OCS Topology Design

Workload-static OCS maps the recurring collective communication demands of distributed decode onto optical circuits configured once at deployment time. Different model regions, notably attention and MoE/FFN, induce distinct logical connectivity requirements over the same multi-port accelerators. We jointly plan the corresponding logical overlays, collective schedules, and their embedding into the physical fabric, deriving fixed OCS configurations and precomputed accelerator routing tables. Communication may involve data relay through intermediate accelerators, allowing the fixed circuits to support multiple logical topologies. We consider rail-optimized two-level scale-up fabrics Wang et al. (2024), whose physical construction is detailed in Appendix C.7.

3.1 Static Communication Demand in Decode

We consider a prefill/decode-disaggregated deployment in which the scale-up fabric serves autoregressive decode. At deployment time, an inference framework selects the model, accelerator allocation, parallelization scheme (such as Helix or DP/TP/EP) and degrees (e.g. TP4 EP8), and operating targets such as maximum context length and interactivity. For a fixed configuration, the communication demand of each decode step is known structurally: participating rank groups, mesh axes, collective primitives, and invocation counts are determined by the model and parallelization. Payloads may depend on batch size and expert routing, but the communication support, the set of possible communicating rank pairs, required by the topology remains fixed.

Inference frameworks already select a collective implementation from a set of viable options: TensorRT-LLM picks between one-shot, two-shot and NCCL all-reduce from offline-tuned tables keyed on tensor-parallel group size, hidden size and token count. As scale-up domains grow, additional factors, such as placement-dependent latency, will have to be factored in. Workload-static switching as described here is a more systematic approach to optimize network communication under the same constraints.

We use Helix-style distributed decode Bhatia et al. (2025), which induces different communication demands across model regions. Attention uses KV-parallel (KVP) and tensor-parallel (TPA) axes, whereas the MoE/FFN region uses expert-parallel (EP) and tensor-parallel (TPE) axes over the same accelerators. Table 1 illustrates the resulting demand: its structural columns are deployment-static, while batch size changes the payload per collective invocation. The KVP all-to-all exchanges partial attention outputs and log-sum-exp statistics across KV-cache shards, as required by Helix-style attention parallelism. Some axes induce no communication in a given region. In this configuration, context length affects KV-cache computation and memory traffic, but not the collective structure or payload.

Token routing may change traffic volume across peers, but need not change the communication support. Our evaluated expert axis uses fixed-group collectives with buffers padded to the busiest expert-parallel rank, so FFN payloads need not scale linearly with batch size (Appendix B.2). Other implementations can regularize routing-dependent traffic through padding or bucketing, at the cost of additional traffic (Appendix A.4). Thus, the fabric can be planned against recurring collective demands rather than topology-agnostic worst-case connectivity.

3.2 From Communication Demand to Logical Topology

We convert the static communication demand of an inference decode forward pass into logical communication graphs. Table 1 gives a worked example of such a demand pattern. Each graph corresponds to one mesh axis in one decode region; its vertices are the participating accelerator ranks, and its edges are the direct communication links available to the collective schedule. The topology planner embeds these graphs into the physical accelerator links.

Since different decode regions induce different logical meshes over the same accelerators, these graphs must be embedded jointly into a shared physical host graph. Its circuits remain fixed during serving, while different regions may reuse them through different logical views.

For power-of-two accelerator counts, we describe logical overlays through Cayley-style graphs. Ranks are labeled by bit strings, and generators connect ranks whose labels differ by a fixed mask. Unit generators yield cube-like structures; additional generators introduce folds or chords that reduce diameter. Folds extend the idea of short-circuiting ring collectives Hammer et al. (2025): instead of reconfiguring the OCS per collective step, the shortcut circuits are provisioned once at deployment, so their cost is accelerator port degree rather than reconfiguration delay on the critical path. Different mesh axes can thus be viewed as different partitions or colorings of one shared host graph, allowing several phase-specific logical topologies to be served by one workload-static set of optical circuits. Figure 2(a) illustrates this for a Q4Q_{4}-style host graph: the same physical connectivity induces different logical mesh views by changing the partition of rank-label bits. Appendix A.1 gives the formal construction.

3.3 Port Allocation as Latency/Bandwidth Trade-off

The previous subsections turn a decode workload into a set of axis requirements over a shared accelerator set. We now expose the main degree of freedom of OCS-based scale-up fabrics with multi-port accelerators: each accelerator has a finite port budget LL, and every port can be spent either to reduce the number of serialized communication phases or to increase bandwidth along an already selected logical edge.

For one logical axis ii, assume a regular overlay of degree did_{i} and uniform edge multiplicity pip_{i}, i.e., each logical edge on that axis is realized by pip_{i} parallel circuits. We estimate a collective schedule with a Hockney-style model

Ti≈hi​λi+vipi​R,T_{i}\approx h_{i}\lambda_{i}+\frac{v_{i}}{p_{i}R}, (1)

where hih_{i} is the number of serialized schedule phases, λi\lambda_{i} is the per-phase accelerator-to-accelerator latency along the selected physical path, viv_{i} is the bottleneck volume, and RR is the bandwidth of one physical link. For an EPS path, λi\lambda_{i} includes the latency of the electronic switch stages traversed; for an OCS path, it includes endpoint, link, and optical pass-through latency. Folds reduce hih_{i} by shortening the logical graph; parallel circuits increase pip_{i} and reduce serialization time, as shown in Figures 2(b) and 2(c).

More generally, let H=(V,E)H=(V,E) denote the physical host graph and pep_{e} the multiplicity of edge ee. Since each circuit consumes one port at its endpoint, the per-accelerator port budget is

∑e∈δ⁡(u)pe≤L∀u∈V,\sum_{e\in\delta(u)}p_{e}\leq L\qquad\forall u\in V, (2)

where δ⁡(u)\delta(u) is the set of edges incident to accelerator uu.

For disjoint axis-specific edge families of degree did_{i} and uniform multiplicity pip_{i}, this simplifies to ∑idi​pi≤L\sum_{i}d_{i}p_{i}\leq L. In the shared-host construction, physical edges reused across different logical views are counted only once. Thus, the OCS fabric exposes an explicit exchange rate between latency and bandwidth: ports spent on additional generators make the graph shallower (hi↓h_{i}\downarrow), while ports spent on multiplicity make selected edges wider (pi↑p_{i}\uparrow).

A fold that reduces the schedule by Δ​h\Delta h phases saves approximately Δ​h​λi\Delta h\lambda_{i}, provided the schedule exploits it. Increasing multiplicity from pip_{i} to pi+1p_{i}+1 instead saves vi/[R​pi​(pi+1)]v_{i}/[Rp_{i}(p_{i}+1)].

With a locally linear volume model vi≈ci​mv_{i}\approx c_{i}m, where mm is the number of tokens per forward pass and cic_{i} the bottleneck volume per token, the crossover occurs at

mi⋆≈Δ​h​λi​R​pi​(pi+1)ci.m_{i}^{\star}\approx\frac{\Delta h\lambda_{i}Rp_{i}(p_{i}+1)}{c_{i}}. (3)

Below this threshold, reducing schedule depth is preferable; above it, additional bandwidth becomes more valuable. High-interactivity decode therefore favors latency-shaped topologies for many, but not necessarily all, axes.

3.4 Collectives as Topology-Specific Schedules

A logical topology improves collective performance only if the communication schedule exploits its connectivity. We describe each collective implementation by a logical overlay, a validity predicate specifying which overlays support the collective, and an ordered schedule of communication phases. Each phase specifies communicating rank pairs, the logical edges used, payload slices, and dependencies on preceding phases. The schedule determines the serialized phase count, bottleneck volume, and link utilization for the analytical model, as well as the communication events initiated by a network simulator (such as Simlette, see Section 5).

We have implemented a planner, conceptually part of the inference deployment framework, which jointly searches over axis partitions, folding generators, edge multiplicities, and compatible collective schedules under the shared accelerator port budget. It selects the topology–schedule combination minimizing predicted communication time for the deployment’s target message-size regime. Folds reduce latency only when schedules exploit their additional connectivity, while parallel circuits improve bandwidth only when schedules distribute traffic across them. Appendix A.2 details the topology search, and Appendix A.3 describes the topology-aware collective algorithms.

4 gxnet: Workload Modeling for Distributed LLM Decode

gxnet converts a model-level computation graph and a deployment, i.e., accelerator specification, system size, precision, and parallelization strategy, into a shape-exact distributed decode execution with explicit compute regions, memory traffic, collectives, device groups, and timing dependencies. It provides the deployment-time communication demand for topology planning and the timed execution for network simulation. Appendix B provides additional details.

4.1 Model Graph and Sharding Transformations

One decode step is a computation graph whose tensors carry shape, element type, and logical device placement. A decode step is specialized to generating one token (or verifying multiple tokens) per active request against an existing KV cache. Communication is derived structurally from this placement: wherever adjacent operators require different tensor placements, gxnet inserts a collective, whose group follows from the mesh axes, payload from tensor shape and element width, and occurrence count from the layer structure. For a fixed model and parallelization, this yields the deployment-time demand of Table 1 before execution.

The same sharded graph yields the per-rank weight and KV-cache footprint, which bounds the batch size feasible in accelerator memory. For MoE regions, we model dropless routing that is uniform in expectation: routing affects expert compute and FFN collective payloads, but not collective group membership; routing skew is not modeled.

4.2 Per-rank Execution Trace and Cost Model

gxnet lowers the communication-explicit graph into a per-rank execution trace, akin to traces recorded on real hardware with tools such as Chakra Sridharan et al. (2026): the compute regions, memory accesses, collectives, and dependencies a single accelerator carries out or is exposed to during a decode step. Where a collective schedule (Section 3.4) describes how one collective uses a logical overlay, the trace determines when collectives occur, which ranks participate, what payload they carry, and whether their latency is exposed or hidden behind computation.

The dependency representation can express communication–computation overlap. We use Helix’s attention/FFN sharding without HOP-B, i.e., without splitting attention into microbatches whose all-to-all overlaps with the attention of the next, so communication latency is fully exposed in the decode-step timeline. A sensitivity analysis (Appendix B.5) shows that HOP-B does not improve decode-step time in the evaluated configurations: for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, microbatching adds more all-to-all communication than HOP-B can hide, and for Megatron 5T, it yields no net benefit.

Each compute region’s execution time is estimated with a roofline model taking the maximum of compute time and HBM-transfer time, using tensor-derived FLOPs and bytes together with size-dependent compute and memory efficiencies. Operators between communication points are grouped into fused execution windows and charged one launch overhead per window. Exact efficiency functions and accelerator parameters are given in Appendix B.3, and Appendix D.3 relates the model to kernel measurements on current hardware.

gxnet is analytical rather than cycle-accurate; projected accelerators use specification-level throughput and bandwidth parameters, while measured kernel durations can replace analytical estimates for existing hardware.

4.3 Coupling gxnet to the Network Model

gxnet interfaces with the network model at two points. Before execution, it emits the complete communication demand of a decode step, against which the OCS fabric of Section 3 is mapped and routed once at setup. In practice, an inference framework such as vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) or SGLang Zheng et al. (2024), which already holds this information, would perform this step. During execution, gxnet registers each collective with its group, primitive, payload, axis, and earliest start time. It does so until all further events in its scheduler are blocked by dependencies to pending/registered collective operations. It then calls an advance function to delegate control to the network simulator. The network simulator returns the collective’s actual start and completion time on the specified network topology and for the given collective schedule. Once the completion time is known, dependent operators in gxnet’s internal scheduler are released. Whether a collective is exposed on the decode critical path is thus determined by the coupled execution, not by summing independently timed messages.

All collective instances whose dependencies are satisfied may be in flight simultaneously; Simlette advances them jointly and therefore captures contention and credit stalls between concurrent groups, whereas the analytical backend estimates collectives independently. A run produces a timed decode-step timeline, from which we derive token-to-token latency, per-user interactivity, and system throughput, and, with the power model of Appendix D.4, energy-normalized throughput.

5 Communication Model and Grounding

Evaluating workload-static OCS fabrics requires estimating the completion time of collective communication kernels on hardware and topologies that are not yet available at scale. We use two models for this: a fast analytical model to evaluate candidate topologies and schedules, and a flit-level simulator to capture effects that the analytical model misses, such as credit stalls and link contention. Both use latency parameters based on measurements from current hardware.

5.1 Simlette: a Flit-Level Event-Based Simulator

We evaluate collective schedules and routing on EPS and OCS fabrics using Simlette, a discrete-event simulator built on SimPy Team SimPy (). Inspired by the UALink specification Ultra Accelerator Link Consortium (2025), it models memory-semantic transactions at flit granularity, capturing serialization, link contention, and credit stalls during execution. Simlette supports single-level and two-level spine-leaf fabrics, dynamic EPS packet switching and spraying, and workload-static OCS routing without runtime reconfiguration.

The simulator separates workload mapping into four independent layers: physical topology, worker allocation, collective schedule, and routing (Appendix C.1). This modular design allows us to vary each component independently while keeping the others fixed, enabling controlled comparisons of fabrics, placements, schedules, and routing strategies.

5.2 UALink Transactions and Credit-Based Flow Control

Simlette implements the transaction and credit-based flow control system of the UALink specification, the same mechanisms used in practice for direct accelerator-to-accelerator communication. Each transaction pairs a request (e.g., a read or a write) issued by an Originator with the response returned by a Completer. One or more 64-byte Transaction Layer (TL) flits are grouped into a 640-byte Data Link (DL) flit before being put on the link, and switching and flow control operate at DL-flit granularity. Each port maintains independent credit channels for request and response traffic, so that traffic in one direction can never block the other. A port must hold a credit on the corresponding channel before sending a DL flit; credits are returned once the receiver has processed the data, so a buffer is never sent more data than it can store.

5.3 Latency Decomposition

The fixed per-hop latency is divided into four components: endpoint latency inside the accelerator (processor to cache to scale-up port), protocol latency of the scale-up port including credit transmission, link propagation delay, and switch forwarding delay.

For the latency comparison, we apply common endpoint, protocol, and propagation parameters, while distinguishing EPS forwarding (approx. 300 ns (64, Sec. 10.9.2) unloaded pin-to-pin latency) from OCS optical pass-through (approx. 10 ns).

Figure 3 shows the latency of a 512-accelerator all-reduce on an example single-level fabric. The buffer size is the amount of data, in bytes, that each accelerator holds at the end of the collective. For the low-batch payloads of Table 1 (4 to 64 KiB), switch latency accounts for about a third of each EPS bar, while OCS removes almost all of it (2 % of the bar).

For buffers of 1 to 64 KiB, which cover the low-batch payloads of Table 1, the completion time is 3.18–3.26 μ\mus for OCS, compared with 5.21–5.26 μ\mus for EPS. As the payload grows beyond 64 KiB, serialization takes over on OCS, reaching 41 % of the time at 1 MiB (2.07 μ\mus), where OCS remains faster with 5.10 μ\mus compared with 6.41 μ\mus for EPS.

5.4 Analytical Model and Consistency Checks

The analytical model times each candidate port allocation of Section 3.3 by Eq. (1), with the bottleneck volume vv obtained as the sum over all phases of the data carried by the most loaded edge (Appendix C.2). Simlette then builds the circuits of the allocation with the lowest predicted time and simulates the collectives on them flit by flit, including credit waits and the load on each link.

The analytical model assumes that phases do not overlap, that no transfer shares its link with another, and that a sender never waits for buffer space at the receiver. Without contention and with unlimited buffers, Simlette reproduces the analytical completion time for all message sizes and radices on a single-level OCS fabric (Appendix C.4). When the buffer per port is too small to keep a link busy for one hop, senders wait for credits and Simlette results are up to 1.9×1.9\times slower; when several flows reach the same switch port, as for the two-shot all-reduce on EPS, the analytical model underestimates completion time by up to 2×2\times.

The analytical model is accurate for contention-free schedules with sufficient buffering. Simlette captures additional delays from credit stalls and concurrent traffic, which the analytical model omits. We therefore use the analytical model for design-space exploration and Simlette to evaluate the selected configurations with a more detailed representation of contention and credit effects.

5.5 Grounding

We parameterize Simlette using hardware measurements and published interconnect specifications (Appendix C.6). Custom accelerator-to-accelerator ping-pong kernels estimate end-to-end communication latency, while pointer-chasing microbenchmarks characterize the local memory hierarchy Luo et al. (2025). On NVIDIA Blackwell B300 for example, memory-hierarchy measurements yield access latencies of approximately 14 ns (shared memory), 17 ns (L1), and 140 ns (L2), compared with a measured accelerator-to-accelerator remote-access round trip of 1.61 μ\mus. These measurements constrain the accelerator-side latency budget, while the attribution of the remaining latency to protocol, interconnect, and switching components requires additional modeling assumptions (Appendix C.6). We characterize accelerator-to-accelerator latency using several ping-pong kernel implementations, and we select the minimum measured duration as a minimum upper bound. Appendix C.6 details further measurements and implementation-dependent variation.

End-to-end measurements do not uniquely determine the latency contribution of every internal component. We therefore state the assumed component latencies explicitly and examine their influence through the sensitivity analysis of Appendix E. Simlette produces deterministic completion times for the specified hardware and workload parameters; run-to-run jitter and tail-latency distributions are outside the scope of this evaluation.

6 Evaluation

We first present results for two model architectures, Megatron 5T MoE and GPT-OSS-5.3-like, for very large context lengths of 5 million tokens. The choice of large models with large context is motivated by current hardware limitations and the resulting need to scale to fabrics larger than what a single datacenter rack can provide, even with accelerators such as the upcoming Vera Rubin platforms NVIDIA (). Model architectures and accelerator properties are given in Appendices D.1 and D.3.

6.1 Optimized Interactivity-Throughput Envelope

Figure 4 plots achieved interactivity, the per-user throughput metric, against total system throughput for various batch sizes. A batch of 16 concurrent users is the largest that the 512 serving accelerators can hold for Megatron before KV cache pages have to be swapped out of an accelerator’s HBM. The three network scenarios are two-level networks using only EPS (all-EPS), OCS on the second level (hybrid EPS/OCS), or only OCS (all-OCS); the first two are 4:1 oversubscribed towards the second level, while all-OCS is non-blocking (Appendix C.7). The EPS-based fabrics use 4:1 leaf-to-spine oversubscription to maintain a practical system-power envelope. A sensitivity experiment with GPT-OSS-5.3-like at batch size 1 shows that removing oversubscription requires four times as many spine switches (288 vs. 72), yet reduces collective completion time by only 3.2 % (13.61 to 13.18 μ\mus). Consistently, the bandwidth sensitivity in Figure 28 from Appendix E shows that even quadrupling per-port bandwidth barely changes the all-OCS interactivity advantage (64.8 % to 62.8 %), supporting the interpretation that the observed gains are primarily latency-driven rather than an artifact of EPS oversubscription.

The Pareto front for each scenario is found by searching the Helix parallelization space (Appendix B.6), so the optimal parallelization for a given batch size may differ between fabrics: reduced collective completion time can make a higher degree of parallelism along a mesh dimension viable. For instance, batch size 1 on Megatron calls for a Helix scheme (KVP4, TPA128, EP16, TPE32) on all-EPS, reaching 458 tokens/s/user, while all-OCS reaches 698 tokens/s/user with (KVP4, TPA128, EP8, TPE64). The larger FFN tensor-parallel group is enabled by our collective schedule optimization for large groups, whereas a group of 64 on this physical topology forces EPS traffic through both levels, and thus three switching devices.

6.2 Bottlenecks Change with Batch Size

In high-interactivity/low-batch regimes of Figure 4, collective communication volume is small and network latency contributes substantially to decode-step time, so the difference between all-EPS and all-OCS fabrics is significant: for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, 775 versus 1277 tokens/s/user, 1.65×\times the interactivity. In practice, achievable values may be lower due to unmodeled system properties such as accelerator-to-accelerator jitter or GEMM inefficiencies for certain operand aspect ratios; on the other hand, this analysis does not factor in EPS-specific disadvantages such as tail latency due to buffer congestion and arbitration delays. The lower power consumption of OCS fabrics further amplifies their advantage, so the energy per generated token decreases through both lower system power and faster token generation.

As batch size increases, compute kernel time and network transaction sizes grow, which reduces the share of exposed latency in the token generation time (time per output token, TPOT). Figure 5 shows that this effect is strong for Megatron but weak for GPT-OSS-5.3-like. Attention time scales with the KV bytes read per decode step, i.e., with the product of batch size and context length. Megatron keeps 1 MiB of KV cache per token of context, GPT-OSS-5.3-like only 48 KiB, since its interleaved sliding-window attention reads the full context in only half of its layers, with 16 instead of 128 KV heads (Table 10, Appendix D.1); the hidden size, 8192 in both models, does not explain the difference. At 5M context, Megatron’s attention time therefore grows from 0.53 ms at batch 1 to 8.3 ms at batch 16, while communication stays nearly constant, so the OCS saving of 0.71 to 0.74 ms per step falls from 34 % to 7 % of the all-EPS step. For GPT-OSS-5.3-like, attention reaches only 0.41 ms, and communication remains the largest term throughout. The remainder of each step is the fixed invocation cost of its fused execution windows (Section 4), identical across fabrics and batch sizes.

6.3 Scaling and Energy Efficiency

Figure 6 shows the scaling with system size for each of the three physical topologies; each point is again the result of a parallelization search. The maximum context is fixed at 64K tokens to allow scaling across a range of world sizes; after all, growing scale-up domains is not always motivated by higher interactivity but may also be required to provide more low-latency, high-bandwidth memory. At batch sizes 1 and 4, interactivity first rises with world size and then falls once collectives span the second level: all-EPS peaks at 64 accelerators, all-OCS only at 128, 26 % and 41 % higher than the all-EPS peak. At batch 16, all-OCS fabrics show the most favorable interactivity, and thus throughput, scaling, reaching 1.5×\times the interactivity of all-EPS at 512 accelerators.

Finally, Figure 7 takes a broader perspective across three scenarios of model size and maximum context length. Small models with small context are usually the free-tier variants that AI providers offer, while large models with long context are a paid service because they aim to provide high-value work such as agent supervision and long-term reasoning. Instead of total system throughput, the y-axis shows tokens per second per megawatt, the perspective of datacenter operators whose token volume, and thus profitability, is usually limited by available power. The proposed scheme is of general utility across the three very different regimes evaluated here: owing to the lower per-port power of OCS (Appendix D.4), all-OCS fabrics outperform their EPS counterparts in throughput per unit energy by 35 to 37 % even for the 8- and 16-accelerator deployments of Megatron 235B and 1T, where interactivity improves by only 1 to 3 %, and by up to 102 % in the high-value, large-model regime where the interactivity advantage rises to 52 %; across the GPT-OSS family, the energy efficiency gain ranges from 32 to 119 % (Appendix D.2). GPT-OSS-5.3-like at batch 1 is also the baseline of the sensitivity analysis over per-port bandwidth, accelerator radix, and switch and accelerator latency in Appendix E.

7 Discussion and Conclusion

Distributed LLM decode exhibits recurring collective communication patterns that can be served by optical circuits configured once per deployment. We show that jointly optimizing circuit connectivity, accelerator port allocation, and topology-aware collective schedules allows OCS-based fabrics to support these patterns without runtime reconfiguration. Allocating ports to reduce communication phases or increase effective bandwidth improves modeled interactivity and energy efficiency over EPS-based fabrics, particularly in latency-sensitive decode regimes. For Megatron 5T MoE, all-OCS fabrics improve modeled interactivity by up to 52 % and energy efficiency by up to 102 % over the oversubscribed all-EPS baseline; for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, the corresponding improvements reach 65 % and 119 %.

Given a physical fabric and accelerator port budget, our planner constructs candidate logical overlays from Cayley-graph generators. It jointly explores mesh-axis partitions, shortcut connections that reduce collective schedule depth, and parallel circuits that increase bandwidth. Compatible collective schedules are evaluated using an analytical latency–bandwidth model, and the configuration minimizing workload-weighted communication time is mapped onto physical ports as a deployment-static circuit topology.

These benefits of our approach are conditional on the workload and hardware assumptions. Their magnitude depends on the communication exposed on the decode critical path, accelerator endpoint latency, model architecture, and the power and oversubscription assumptions of the compared fabrics. With co-packaged optics (CPO), accelerators may see a rise in both per-port data rates, e.g., through WDM-capable optical PHYs such as OCI OCI MSA (2026), and port count (accelerator radix). Both can be shown to improve the benefits of workload-static switching in terms of system performance and energy efficiency (Appendix E).

Our main evaluation excludes compute–communication overlap, although HOP-B microbatching is examined separately (Appendix B.5). We also assume balanced expert routing and do not model routing skew or stochastic execution-time variations.

More broadly, our results motivate treating scale-up topology, model parallelization, and collective schedules as a joint optimization problem, including for optically switched fabrics. Future work should validate the predicted performance and energy benefits on physical hardware, extend the optimization to overlapping computation and communication, and assess robustness to dynamic traffic and routing imbalance. Workload-static OCS thus offers a promising alternative to general-purpose packet switching when communication requirements are predictable at deployment time.

Appendix A Workload-Static Topology and Collective Design

This appendix details the workload-static topology design and collective schedules. It covers graph construction, joint topology–schedule optimization, and variable MoE traffic, followed by worked examples, fabric comparisons, alternative port allocations, and limitations.

Throughout this appendix we use the notation of Section 3 and drop the axis index ii where only one axis is considered: hh is the number of serialized schedule phases, λ\lambda the per-phase latency, vv the bottleneck volume, pp the edge multiplicity, RR the bandwidth of one physical link, and mm the number of tokens per forward pass. We denote the payload of one collective call by σ\sigma, with σ=c​m\sigma=c\,m for a per-token volume cc; we also call it the buffer size of the collective, i.e., the larger of its input and output buffers (Section 3.1). It differs from the messages a schedule sends: each phase transfers per-port messages whose sizes are determined by the schedule and, e.g., for coset-factored schedules, are not uniform across phases.

A.1 Shared-Host Graph Construction

Under Helix parallelism Bhatia et al. (2025), every layer of a decode step passes through a sequence of regions, each of which arranges the same NN accelerators into its own logical device mesh (Figure 8). The attention region uses a mesh of shape (KVP, TPA) and ends in an all-to-all over its KV-parallel axis; the output projection is followed by an all-reduce over a one-dimensional mesh spanning all accelerators; and the FFN/MoE region uses a mesh of shape (TPE, EP), with a tensor-parallel all-reduce and an expert-parallel all-gather. Each dimension of a mesh is a mesh axis, and its extents form the mesh shape. The accelerators that differ only in their coordinate along one axis form a collective group of that axis, so in a two-axis mesh every accelerator belongs to exactly two collective groups, one per axis.

Helix is one of several parallelization schemes for decode, and its region structure is more demanding than that of the common TP/EP scheme. There, attention and FFN typically share one mesh and one tensor-parallel axis; under Helix, the attention and FFN meshes split the same accelerators along different axes, since TPE generally differs from TPA. The shared-host allocation must therefore serve several conflicting mesh shapes with one host graph, in which every mesh axis uses a subgraph and the subgraphs of different meshes share edges. The subgraphs have to be chosen in conjunction with the collective schedules, since a densely connected logical topology only pays off where a schedule can exploit its additional edges. We build every subgraph from a hypercube spanning the collective groups of its axis, the regular topology in which each of 2a2^{a} accelerators has one link per dimension to aa neighbors. Hypercubes suit this purpose because the hypercubes of all mesh axes are sub-cubes of one hypercube spanning all accelerators, so a single wiring serves every mesh shape. To them we add either folds, i.e., shortcuts across the cube that lower its diameter, or parallel circuits that raise its bandwidth, both at the cost of additional ports. Choosing them for all meshes at once is a joint optimization problem, in which the alignment of folds across meshes (Appendix A.1) and the joint choice of partitions and folds (Appendix A.2) become necessary.

Bit labels, cosets, and the hypercube invariant

We label each of the N=2nN=2^{n} accelerators with its index in binary. A generator is an nn-bit mask gg that induces the edge x↔x⊕gx\leftrightarrow x\oplus g at every node. A set SS of generators thus defines the Cayley graph Cay⁡((ℤ2)n,S)\operatorname{Cay}((\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{n},S) of the group of nn-bit labels under bitwise XOR: its vertices are the labels, and every label xx is connected to x⊕sx\oplus s for each s∈Ss\in S Godsil and Royle (2001). Since every label is its own inverse under XOR, the edges are undirected. Three standard properties of such graphs are used throughout: for distinct non-zero generators, the graph is |S||S|-regular, i.e., every node has one neighbor per generator; it is vertex-transitive, i.e., it looks identical from every node, so per-node port counts and schedules carry over to all nodes; and it is connected exactly when SS spans (ℤ2)n(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{n}. We write labels and masks as bit strings, most significant bit first, so that a label reads x=bn−1​…​b0x=b_{n-1}\dots b_{0}; the generator g=111g=111, for instance, sets bits 0, 1 and 2 and connects every label xx to x⊕111x\oplus 111, i.e., to the label with these three bits flipped. The unit masks ej=2je_{j}=2^{j} generate the hypercube QnQ_{n}, whose degree and diameter are both nn and whose graph distance is the Hamming distance (Table 2).

A 2-D mesh of shape (2a0,2a1)(2^{a_{0}},2^{a_{1}}) partitions the bit positions into two blocks. The coordinate of a node along an axis is the value of that axis’s bits, and a collective group is the set of nodes that agree on all bits outside the block. Each group is therefore a coset of the block subgroup: there are N/siN/s_{i} of them, each of size si=2ais_{i}=2^{a_{i}}. This is why we restrict axis extents to powers of two: grid coordinate and label slice become the same object. Other sizes could be handled by planning the enclosing power of two and marking the surplus labels as absent, which we do not implement.

Unit masks over disjoint blocks together form the unit-mask set of the larger cube. For N=16N=16, the meshes (2,8)=Q1​□​Q3(2,8)=Q_{1}\,\square\,Q_{3} and (4,4)=Q2​□​Q2(4,4)=Q_{2}\,\square\,Q_{2} are therefore the same 32-edge cube Q4Q_{4}, colored into axes in two different ways (Figure 2(a)). One fixed wiring thus serves every power-of-two mesh shape at diameter nn. Every other configuration the shared-host planner considers keeps this cube as its base and only adds to it, either additional generators that fold it (Appendix A.1) or parallel circuits that widen its edges.

The planner treats the bit partition of each mesh as its placement decision and chooses it jointly with the folds (Appendix A.2).

Table 3 summarizes the topologies a single axis could take. Reducing the degree below d=ad=a differs qualitatively from increasing it: the axis can no longer remain in (ℤ2)a(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{a} and has to change group. The shared-host planner therefore stays in the cube family, d≥ad\geq a; rings and circulants appear only in the stacked-link allocation of Appendix A.6 and for a ring schedule on a single mesh (Appendix A.5.1).

Folding generators, the support rule, and alignment

The hypercube uses nn ports per accelerator, one per unit mask. Any further port, i.e., a host degree D>nD>n, can be spent on an additional generator of Hamming weight at least two. Whereas a unit mask connects labels that differ in a single bit, a generator of weight ww connects labels that differ in ww bits at once, a pair the cube alone separates by ww hops. Such generators act as chords that fold the cube. Adding g=111g=111 to an axis of size 8 makes antipodal nodes adjacent, raising the degree from 3 to 4 and lowering the diameter from 3 to 2 (Figure 9). Whether a fold helps a given axis is governed by its support: a folding generator only helps a mesh axis if all of its set bits lie inside that axis’s bit block. If its support spans two blocks, the circuits are still built and occupy ports, but the collectives of that mesh leave them idle.

Since a generator adds one port on every node, folds are a global resource shared by all meshes, and they are the main source of coupling between them. For N=16N=16 with the concurrent mesh shapes (2,8)(2,8) and (4,4)(4,4) and their partitions b3|b2​b1​b0b_{3}\mid b_{2}b_{1}b_{0} and b3​b2|b1​b0b_{3}b_{2}\mid b_{1}b_{0} of Figure 2(a), the mask 00110011 lies inside axis B of both meshes and reduces the diameter of both from 4 to 3. The mask 11001100 helps only (4,4)(4,4), whose axis A it turns into K4K_{4}; it leaves (2,8)(2,8) at diameter 4, since that partition places bits 3 and 2 on different axes. Together, the two masks bring (4,4)(4,4) to diameter 2 and (2,8)(2,8) to 3 (Figure 10). Choosing partitions such that one chord serves the latency-bound axes of several meshes is therefore a genuine optimization problem, and the reason why partitions are part of the search.

Two cases simplify the problem. With a single mesh there is nothing to align to, so an axis could leave the cube family, e.g., become a degree-2 ring that frees ports for edge multiplicity; our planner offers this only to the ring schedule, which it can evaluate, since an analytical cost model exists, but which the simulator does not execute (Table 7). This is because in the latency-bound inference decode regime, the ring algorithm typically is the worst of all schedule choices. A logical-only axis, i.e., a mesh dimension that carries no collective, such as a replica or pipeline-stage axis, receives neither circuits nor collective groups. Its bits still label nodes so that the other axes can index their cosets by them, but the ports it would otherwise occupy remain available.

Realizing the host graph: edge coloring

Mapping the host graph onto the OCS planes is an edge coloring problem in which colors correspond to ports. For a Cayley graph of (ℤ2)n(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{n}, this coloring is immediate: the edges {x,x⊕g}\{x,x\oplus g\} of one generator gg form a perfect matching, so coloring every edge by its generator is proper and uses exactly DD colors, and each of the pep_{e} circuits of a multiplied edge receives its own copy of that color. Every aligned host graph therefore fits the port budget of Eq. (2) without a coloring search, whatever the weights of its generators. Only when the combined demand graph is not a Cayley graph of (ℤ2)n(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{n}, for instance for meshes that are not aligned to one host, can it require one color more than its maximum degree (Vizing’s theorem); a port then has to be reserved.

A.2 Joint Topology–Schedule Optimization

The impact of folds and multiplicity

The planner spends the ports of Eq. (2) on two resources: fold generators, which cost one port per node and reduce the phase count hh of the axes whose schedules can use them, and parallel circuits, which raise the multiplicity pp of an axis. Each axis is evaluated using Eq. (1), where hh counts the phases the selected schedule actually traverses, not the graph diameter, and an axis completes at the pace of its least-multiplied generator, its effective multiplicity pip_{i}. An edge shared by several axes takes the largest multiplicity any of them requires; together with the global nature of folds, this is the only coupling between meshes. The planner minimizes ∑iwi​Ti\sum_{i}w_{i}T_{i} subject to Eq. (2), where wiw_{i} counts how often axis ii’s collective occurs per decode step.

The diameter frontier and the schedulable frontier

The number of phases a given degree can buy is a staircase (Figure 11). The diameter frontier bounds every schedule; the schedulable frontier of the coset-factored schedules (Appendix A.3) lags behind it, because these schedules need generator sets that factor into non-overlapping layers: on an axis of 64 accelerators, diameter 2 is reached at degree 13, but two coset layers only at degree 14. Both frontiers are precomputed per axis size.

Search structure and the planner

The planner proceeds in the stages of Figure 12: it selects candidate schedules per axis, derives each axis’s ladder of candidate folds from its schedule, searches bit partitions, fold sets and multiplicities jointly, and colors the resulting circuits onto ports. For large instances, the search is heuristic. The planner is deterministic, so a plan is a pure function of its request and can be cached and reused.

Binding the cost model to execution

The cost model is only trustworthy if hh and vv are properties of the actual schedule rather than of an idealization of it. We therefore specify every collective implementation as a triple of an executable schedule, a validity predicate, and a closed-form cost (Section 3.4), and check that the three agree. The closed-form cost takes the topology and the payload and returns (h,v,u)(h,v,u): serialized phases, bottleneck-link bytes, and ports driven per node. It does not receive λ\lambda, RR or pp; the planner alone owns these deployment parameters and forms TT by Eq. (1). We run the resulting check for every collective schedule the planner can select: under the assumptions of the closed form, i.e., a fixed per-phase latency λ\lambda, link bandwidth RR, multiplicity p=1p=1 and no competing traffic, the simulated completion time of the schedule has to match h​λ+v/(p​R)h\lambda+v/(pR).

The check prevents two failure modes that would otherwise be undetectable. First, crediting recursive doubling with a folded diameter it cannot use would make the selector prefer it on every folded cube. Second, charging RS+AG a full message per phase instead of its geometric two-shot total would make the selector never choose it. The validity predicate keeps invalid combinations of schedule and topology out of the search entirely, rather than having the cost model extrapolate a value for a schedule that would not run.

The scope of this check is internal consistency between the closed form and a simulated execution of the same schedule under the same idealizing assumptions; it is not a hardware validation. It currently covers p=1p=1 only: with parallel circuits, the closed form is known to over-predict the simulated time, so plans that use p>1p>1 are, if anything, estimated pessimistically. Grounding of the constants themselves (λ\lambda, RR, endpoint and protocol terms) is treated separately in Section 5.5.

A.3 Topology-Aware Collective Schedules

All-reduce operating points

Two lower bounds hold for any all-reduce schedule: the diameter of the topology, since every node’s result depends on all inputs, and ⌈logd+1⁡N⌉\lceil\log_{d+1}N\rceil phases at degree dd. The achievable minimum is the larger of the two.

Recursive doubling cannot use folding edges, since merging partial results with overlapping source sets would count inputs twice. Our coset-factored schedules respect this constraint: they group the generators of a fold into layers S1,…,SℓS_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} that tile the group without overlap, ∏j(1+|Sj|)=N\prod_{j}(1+|S_{j}|)=N, and exchange over one layer per phase, so a fold of ℓ\ell layers needs ℓ\ell phases. On a block fold, these layers are exactly its complete layers (Table 2). Where no such tiling is as short as the diameter, as on Q4+1111Q_{4}{+}1111, the diameter can still be reached by reusing links across phases at a higher volume, as the one-shot schedule does (Table 4). The parallel variant of the coset-factored schedule keeps the ℓ\ell phases and reduces the bottleneck volume from ℓ​σ\ell\sigma to σ\sigma. RS+AG on the same layers trades phases for volume: a reduce-scatter and an all-gather of ℓ\ell phases each, with a volume that shrinks geometrically in the layer radices rj=1+|Sj|r_{j}=1+|S_{j}|, the number of nodes a layer connects,

vrs+ag=2​σ​∑j=1ℓ∏k≤jrk−1,v_{\textsc{rs+ag}}=2\sigma\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\prod_{k\leq j}r_{k}^{-1}, (4)

which on the plain cube is the familiar 2​N−1N​σ2\frac{N-1}{N}\sigma; its parallel variant divides this volume by ℓ\ell on a uniform fold.

The planner selects by arg⁡min⁡T\arg\min T among the schedules whose validity predicate holds and that are not dominated (Table 5). In the latency-bound regime the coset-factored parallel schedule usually wins on the deepest fold the budget affords; in the bandwidth-bound regime parallel RS+AG does, whose volume is lower than σ\sigma but which needs twice as many phases. The worked plan of Appendix A.5.1 illustrates the former. Figure 13 compares the resulting all-reduce completion times with those of the all-EPS fabric over a range of buffer sizes (Appendix A.5.2).

All-to-all

The all-to-all generalizes the radix-rr Bruck algorithm Bruck et al. (1997) to multi-port accelerators on the same coset layers and takes ℓ\ell phases on a fold of ℓ\ell layers. For axes whose number of bits is prime, such as 128 accelerators, uniform folds are scarce, so we additionally admit balanced mixed-radix block folds such as Q7​[4,3]=K16​□​K8Q_{7}[4,3]=K_{16}\,\square\,K_{8} (Table 2); their parallel schedules are priced by the narrowest layer. Figure 13 shows the corresponding all-to-all completion times (Appendix A.5.2).

A.4 Variable MoE Traffic and Regularization

MoE token routing and deterministic all-to-all

The workload-static argument requires the communication of decode to be fixed at deployment time. Token routing is the only mechanism in the model that varies from token to token, so we state here what has to be regularized, what does not, and what regularization costs.

With NexpN_{\mathrm{exp}} experts distributed over NepN_{\mathrm{ep}} expert-parallel groups and top-kk routing, each decode step produces a dispatch traffic matrix W∈ℕNep×NepW\in\mathbb{N}^{N_{\mathrm{ep}}\times N_{\mathrm{ep}}}, whose entry Wu​vW_{uv} counts the rows sent from group uu to group vv; a combine phase with the transposed pattern follows. The router determines the entries of WW, but not its support: no routing decision is excluded a priori, and over any nontrivial number of steps every ordered pair occurs. The logical graph the circuits must serve is therefore the complete graph on the expert-parallel axis, i.e., an all-to-all, independent of the router. The topology can thus be static without any regularization. Regularization is only needed for the schedule, since a fixed phase structure and a fixed planner input both require the per-pair payloads to be fixed.

Capacity padding.

We assign each expert a fixed capacity

C=⌈γ⋅k​mNexp⌉C\;=\;\left\lceil\gamma\cdot\frac{k\,m}{N_{\mathrm{exp}}}\right\rceil (5)

with capacity factor γ≥1\gamma\geq 1, and pad every buffer between a source group and a destination expert to CC rows. Every ordered pair then exchanges exactly C⋅(Nexp/Nep)⋅dmodelC\cdot(N_{\mathrm{exp}}/N_{\mathrm{ep}})\cdot d_{\mathrm{model}} elements per step, independent of the routing outcome, where dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} is the hidden size. The dispatch becomes a uniform all-to-all over the expert-parallel axis that maps directly onto the Bruck/coset schedule of Appendix A.3, with hh and vv fixed and known. Tokens exceeding the capacity are handled on an overflow path outside the static schedule, either dropped, as is common in training, or deferred to the next step. Production inference kernels take the opposite end of this trade-off: they size per-peer receive buffers for the worst case, so that no token is dropped NVIDIA (2026f); vLLM Project (2026b). In our terms, this corresponds to the largest capacity factor, for which padding is only incurred in buffer memory and not necessarily on the wire.

Bucketing.

Padding is the special case of a more general scheme in which per-pair counts are quantized to a small set of levels C1<⋯<CqC_{1}<\dots<C_{q} and the schedule is planned for the largest. Bucketing recovers volume when the routing histogram is reliably skewed, at the cost of qq cached plans instead of one. Since plans are pure functions of their request and are cached (Appendix A.2), the additional planning cost is paid once per bucket at deployment. Our simulator implements neither routing, capacity nor overflow: it runs the dispatch as a uniform all-to-all of the declared per-pair payload, which is exactly the padded dispatch with q=1q=1.

Cost of padding in decode.

Padding increases the bottleneck volume from vv to γ​v\gamma v, so by Eq. (1) the time of the axis becomes T=h​λ+γ​v/(p​R)T=h\lambda+\gamma v/(pR). With v=c​mv=c\,m, the relative penalty is

TγT1= 1+γ−11+h​λ​p​Rv= 1+(γ−1)​mm+m^,m^=h​λ​p​Rc,\frac{T_{\gamma}}{T_{1}}\;=\;1+\frac{\gamma-1}{1+\dfrac{h\lambda pR}{v}}\;=\;1+\frac{(\gamma-1)\,m}{m+\hat{m}},\qquad\hat{m}=\frac{h\lambda pR}{c}, (6)

where m^\hat{m} is the token count at which the latency and bandwidth terms of Eq. (1) are equal. For m≪m^m\ll\hat{m} the penalty vanishes: an axis operating an order of magnitude below m^\hat{m} pays less than 10 % of γ−1\gamma-1. Regularization is therefore affordable in exactly the regime that requires it. At small mm, the routing histogram is least balanced and γ\gamma has to be largest, but this is also where mm is furthest below m^\hat{m}. Conversely, at large batch sizes, where γ\gamma approaches 1 because the histogram concentrates, the axis has moved toward the bandwidth-bound regime in which padding would be expensive. Both effects act in the same direction.

Regularized token routing.

Where an implementation may constrain the router, for instance through balanced assignment or expert-choice routing, the histogram becomes deterministic by construction and γ=1\gamma=1 is attainable without dropping tokens. Since this changes model quality, it is out of scope for this paper; we note it because it removes the only remaining non-determinism in the communication pattern.

What remains variable.

Regularization fixes the dispatch and combine patterns, but not the compute time of the expert MLPs, which still depends on the realized token counts unless the implementation also computes on padding. Similar variability arises from speculative decoding, which varies the number of tokens verified per step and thus compute times and payloads, but not which accelerators communicate. How such variability, and the regularization strategies that bound it, affect the decode step is a question for the workload model (Section 4) rather than for the network model: the circuits serve the collective schedule, whose structure stays fixed, so this variability changes the execution trace but not the network fabric.

A.5 Worked Examples and Fabric Comparisons

A.5.1 Worked Multi-Mesh Plans

A latency-bound multi-mesh plan.

We consider N=256N=256 (n=8n=8) accelerators with L=18L=18 ports, R=5×1010R=5\times 10^{10} B/s (400 Gb/s) and λ=0.52​μ\lambda=0.52\,\mus on a single-level OCS fabric. The fabric serves the mesh (4,64)(4,64) with all-reduce payloads of 4 kB and 32 kB and the mesh (16,16)(16,16) with 4 kB on both axes, and the planner selects every schedule automatically. Every axis is latency-bound, so the budget is spent on degree. The resulting plan has host degree D=17D=17, consisting of the 8 cube generators and 9 folding generators, uses 17 of the 18 ports, and achieves a total of T=4.54​μT=4.54\,\mus (Table 6; Figure 12 traces it through the planner’s stages).

The size-64 axis carries the coset-factored parallel schedule on two complete layers of seven generators each. In terms of Figure 11, it operates at degree 14, the first point of the schedulable frontier with two phases, rather than at degree 13, where the diameter frontier already reaches 2 but no two-layer factorization exists. The size-4 axis is folded into a complete graph and carries the volume-optimized one-shot schedule, which ties with coset-factored parallel there. Both axes of (16,16)(16,16) reach two phases without additional ports: the folds they use are a subset of those already present for (4,64)(4,64), which is why the second axis even receives a degree-8 fold where degree 6 would suffice. The eighteenth port remains unused, since no further fold reduces a phase count and a multiplicity increase on any axis costs at least three ports.

The cost of alignment.

Table 7 contrasts a bandwidth-bound axis with and without a second mesh to align to. With two or more meshes, the fabric is one aligned Q6Q_{6}, so every axis must be a sub-cube and a degree-2 ring is not available. A ring schedule would have to run over a Gray-code Hamiltonian cycle of the Q5Q_{5}, driving only 2 of the 5 links per node; each multiplicity unit then costs 5 ports instead of 2, and the multi-mesh plan reaches p=7p=7 where a single-mesh ring reaches p=17p=17. Alignment costs nothing, however, for the schedule the planner actually selects here. Parallel RS+AG drives all dd links of the cube in every phase, so it gains nothing from a ring and both regimes arrive at the same plan, at half the time of the best ring. The ring schedule serves only as a reference: the planner can evaluate it, but the simulator does not execute it.

A.5.2 Collective Performance Across Fabrics

Figure 13 compares single collectives spanning all 512 accelerators on the two fabrics of Section 6: the all-EPS fabric, two levels and 4:1 oversubscribed towards the second level, with dynamic routing and the schedules of current inference frameworks, and the all-OCS fabric, non-blocking, with the topology and schedule planned for every buffer size.

Every all-reduce on both fabrics is charged at least 2​N−1N​σ2\frac{N-1}{N}\sigma, the volume of a valid sum all-reduce.

For small buffers, both collectives are latency-bound, and all-OCS completes them about twice as fast: a 1 KiB all-reduce takes 1.78 μ\mus instead of 3.77 μ\mus, a 1 KiB all-to-all 1.70 μ\mus instead of 3.02 μ\mus. This advantage does not stem from bandwidth and would therefore persist against a non-blocking EPS fabric. A packet-switched fabric lets any node reach any other, which determines which edges are usable and therefore affects the bandwidth term; it cannot remove serialized phases from a collective, and the switch stages it traverses add to the latency term. Folding instead converts ports into fewer phases. For the all-reduce, the coset-factored parallel schedule is best up to 50 KiB and parallel RS+AG beyond, while the all-EPS fabric moves from one-shot to two-shot and, from 5 MiB on, halving-doubling.

For large buffers, the all-reduce advantage grows to 3.6×3.6\times at 50 MiB (68 instead of 242 μ\mus), which mostly reflects the 4:1 oversubscription of the all-EPS fabric that all-OCS avoids (Appendix C.7); a non-blocking EPS fabric would close most of this part of the gap. For the all-to-all, the advantage peaks at 3.4×3.4\times at 512 KiB (3.05 instead of 10.4 μ\mus) and is 1.84×1.84\times at 250 MiB (0.66 instead of 1.21 ms).

The following Subsection A.5.3 separates the contributions of schedule, subscription, and switch technology to this gap.

A.5.3 Contributions of Schedule, Subscription, and Switch Technology

The EPS fabric of our comparison is oversubscribed 4:1 between its leaf (level-1) and spine (level-2) switches, since a fully subscribed EPS spine with pluggable conversion exceeds a reasonable power envelope; the OCS spine needs no conversion and is fully subscribed. The all-to-all is the collective that suffers most from oversubscription: with CC racks, a fraction (C−1)/C(C-1)/C of every accelerator’s data is addressed to other racks and has to cross the spine, whatever the schedule. To separate the effect of the schedule from that of the fabric, we also run our parallel Bruck schedule on the EPS fabric, with the logical edges of the fold carried as packets over all physical links of each accelerator.

Figure 14 compares four configurations to examine the contributions of collective scheduling, spine subscription, and switch technology. The transition to the fully subscribed EPS reference also changes transport from packet routing to static circuits, so this step does not isolate subscription alone. The EPS fabric at 4:1 with its native all-to-all schedules is the deployment that still fits a reasonable power envelope. Running our parallel Bruck schedule on the same fabric changes only the schedule and accounts for about two thirds of the gap at large buffers: at 250 MiB, it reduces the completion time from 1.21 to 0.85 ms, against 0.66 ms on the OCS fabric. Raising the EPS spine to full subscription changes only the subscription; this configuration can only be built with static circuits, since circuits routed through an EPS spine are colorable only at full bisection, and we include it as a reference that exceeds a reasonable power envelope. At 250 MiB, this step accounts for the remaining third of the gap (0.85 to 0.66 ms). The remaining step replaces the EPS switches of that reference by OCS and changes only the switch technology; at large buffers the two perform alike (0.661 and 0.657 ms at 250 MiB). At small buffers they do not: every hop through an EPS switch still pays its switch latency, so the static reference takes 5.3 instead of 1.8 μ\mus at 1 KiB, which is the latency advantage discussed in Appendix A.5.2. At large buffers, the OCS fabric therefore does not gain on bandwidth at equal subscription. It gains because full subscription is affordable for it, whereas on the EPS fabric the step from 4:1 to 1:1 is exactly the part of the gap that the oversubscribed spine imposes.

A.6 Shared-Host vs. Stacked-Link Allocation

An alternative to the shared-host construction of Section 3.2 is to treat each communication axis independently and allocate it a dedicated subset of accelerator ports. We call this stacked-link allocation. Newer inference hardware architectures devote physical subsets of their scale-up links to a given mesh axis, e.g., TP or EP in TP/EP parallelism Ho et al. (2026). Stacked-link allocation is the workload-aware variant of this concept, which partitions the ports at deployment time rather than at system design time.

Each axis ii receives LiL_{i} ports, with ∑iLi≤L\sum_{i}L_{i}\leq L: one port each, and the rest in proportion to the full-connectivity degree Ni−1N_{i}-1, rounded by largest remainder. If ∑i(Ni−1)≤L\sum_{i}(N_{i}-1)\leq L, every axis is fully connected and the leftover ports become parallel circuits. For each axis over its NiN_{i} ranks, we choose a circulant Cayley graph on ℤNi\mathbb{Z}_{N_{i}} at degree LiL_{i} that minimizes the diameter, using diameter as a latency-oriented proxy for collective completion time. The search is exhaustive for small axes and sampled for large ones, so for large axes the stacked-link circulant is a heuristic, not necessarily the minimum-diameter one. Since a circulant is not a cube, only the one-shot schedules run on it.

Figure 15 compares the two allocation approaches on a single-level OCS fabric of 512 accelerators under an 8 kB all-reduce on a 2-D mesh (8×648\times 64) with 72 collective groups: 64 groups of 8 accelerators along the first axis, and 8 groups of 64 accelerators along the second. The two approaches use the LL links of each accelerator differently. Stacked-link fixes the split beforehand: one set of ports is assigned to the 8-rank axis and another to the 64-rank axis. Each axis can then use its ports only to reduce the diameter of its own graph; until both axes are fully connected, ports assigned to one axis can neither be used by the other nor increase bandwidth. Shared-host instead uses log2⁡N=9\log_{2}N=9 ports to build the base hypercube, whose generators it splits between the two axes, three for the 8-rank axis and six for the 64-rank one. The remaining ports form a common pool, and the planner chooses folds and parallel circuits for both axes jointly under that budget: fold generators to remove collective phases when latency is the main bottleneck, parallel circuits to increase bandwidth when it is. The automatically selected collective schedule then uses whichever the plan provides. This gives shared-host a clear advantage at intermediate radix, from L=16L=16 to L=64L=64 in Figure 15. At higher radix, the two curves converge again: once L≥(8−1)+(64−1)=70L\geq(8-1)+(64-1)=70, stacked-link has enough ports to fully connect both axes independently, and both approaches reach a network diameter of one with the same completion time.

Shared-host allocation is therefore the more efficient in most cases, since one budget serves both axes and surplus ports can go to whichever of latency and bandwidth gains more. Stacked-link allocation is more flexible in the topology it can realize. Our current shared-host construction requires L≥log2⁡NL\geq\log_{2}N, since its base host graph is defined over binary rank labels, and therefore assumes power-of-two axis extents; stacked-link only needs enough ports LiL_{i} per axis to connect its own NiN_{i} ranks. Both allocations determine which logical adjacencies and bandwidth are available to a collective, but neither alone determines the resulting execution time. Their benefits materialize only if the collective schedule can exploit the provided connectivity (Appendix A.3).

A.7 Scope and Limitations

The multi-mesh search is heuristic and does not establish global optimality. Only one- and two-dimensional meshes are supported, all meshes of a deployment must span the same power-of-two world size, and non-power-of-two sizes are not supported at all. The conformance check covers p=1p=1 only (Appendix A.2). The coset-factored schedules require that the partial sums combined in successive phases never overlap, which holds exactly when the generators of a fold tile the group as layers. On irregular folds, such as the diameter-optimal generator set of degree 13 on an axis of size 64, no such tiling exists, so these schedules need more phases than the diameter.

Appendix B Details on gxnet

This appendix details how gxnet translates a model graph into a distributed decode-step execution. It describes the graph transformations, MoE load assumptions, compute and memory cost model, and coupling to the network simulator. It then evaluates sensitivity to HOP-B microbatching and explains the search over parallelization configurations used in the evaluation.

B.1 From Model Graph to Distributed Decode Step

A model graph consists of the token embedding, the decoder layers, and the final norm and LM head. The decoder layers are one repeated block with a repetition count; Megatron 5T repeats one layer, GPT-OSS-5.3-like a pair of a sliding-window and a full-attention layer. Tensor shapes are SymPy expressions in the batch size and in the mesh coordinates of the rank. A sequence of graph-to-graph passes turns the model into a timed distributed decode step:

  1. 1.

    Decode. The graph is specialized to generating one token per user against a KV cache that holds the context.

  2. 2.

    Precision. Activations, weights, and the KV cache are stored in FP4, and collectives communicate activations in FP4; Appendix E repeats the evaluation with BF16 communication.

  3. 3.

    Helix sharding. Attention is placed on a KVP ×\times TPA mesh, which shards the KV cache by sequence over KVP and by KV head over TPA, and the FFN on an EP ×\times TPE mesh over the same accelerators. Collectives are inserted as described in Section 4 (Figure 26).

  4. 4.

    Kernels. Operators are grouped into fused kernels, e.g., the QKV projection, flash-decode attention, and the grouped expert GEMM.
