  5. 5.

    Resources and time. Each kernel is annotated with its FLOPs and HBM traffic, and then with a duration (Appendix B.3).

  6. 6.

    Schedule. Each layer is split into an attention and an FFN region (four regions for GPT-OSS-5.3-like), which execute in order without HOP-B microbatching Bhatia et al. (2025) (Appendix B.5).

The same sharded graph also yields a per-accelerator memory estimate (weights and KV cache), which bounds the batch size that fits in HBM.

B.2 MoE Load Model

Since the all-reduce after the attention output projection replicates the expert input on every accelerator, token routing changes no collective (Section 3.1). It only sets how many tokens each expert processes, and with it the expert compute time and the payload of the TPE all-reduce and EP all-gather. We model dropless routing that is uniform in expectation. With BB users and top-kk routing over NexpN_{\mathrm{exp}} experts, the number of distinct active experts is approximately

Nact=Nexp​(1−(Nexp−1Nexp)B​k),N_{\mathrm{act}}=N_{\mathrm{exp}}\left(1-\left(\tfrac{N_{\mathrm{exp}}-1}{N_{\mathrm{exp}}}\right)^{Bk}\right), (7)

rounded to the nearest integer. The active experts are spread over the EP ranks, so each rank holds ⌊Nact/EP⌋\lfloor N_{\mathrm{act}}/\mathrm{EP}\rfloor or ⌈Nact/EP⌉\lceil N_{\mathrm{act}}/\mathrm{EP}\rceil of them, and its grouped expert GEMM processes ⌈B​k/Nact⌉\lceil Bk/N_{\mathrm{act}}\rceil tokens per active expert. The collectives after the experts carry the rows of the busiest rank, its share of the routed tokens,

R=⌈⌈NactEP⌉​B​kNact⌉,R=\left\lceil\left\lceil\tfrac{N_{\mathrm{act}}}{\mathrm{EP}}\right\rceil\tfrac{Bk}{N_{\mathrm{act}}}\right\rceil, (8)

rounded up once for the rank rather than once per expert. MoE payloads are therefore sublinear in BB (Table 1). We do not model routing skew, which would raise expert compute and payload on the most loaded EP rank.

B.3 Compute and Memory Cost Model

The duration of a kernel is a roofline estimate,

t=max⁡(FPFP4​ηF​(F),DWHBM​ηD​(D)),t=\max\left(\frac{F}{P_{\mathrm{FP4}}\,\eta_{F}(F)},\ \frac{D}{W_{\mathrm{HBM}}\,\eta_{D}(D)}\right), (9)

where FF is the kernel’s FLOPs, DD the bytes it moves to and from HBM, PFP4P_{\mathrm{FP4}} and WHBMW_{\mathrm{HBM}} the peak FP4 throughput and HBM bandwidth of Table 11, and ηF\eta_{F} and ηD\eta_{D} size-dependent efficiencies. For RX00, ηD\eta_{D} is 0.3 for transfers up to 1 MB, 0.6 up to 10 MB, 0.75 up to 100 MB, and 0.9 above; ηF\eta_{F} is 0.15 for kernels up to 7 GFLOP, 0.36 up to 16 GFLOP, 0.53 up to 127 GFLOP, and 0.73 above. A grouped expert kernel reads the weights of every active expert on its rank. The efficiency functions are a step approximation of curves measured on H100 (Appendix D.3).

Kernel launches are charged per rank: the first kernel after each collective pays one launch overhead, and the kernels that follow until the next collective run back to back, as in an accelerator execution graph or persistent-kernel implementation. We use 0.8 μ\mus, the per-kernel gap of a replayed CUDA graph on B200 Cheng et al. (2025).

B.4 Execution and Network Coupling

The schedule is compiled into a plan of compute entries with fixed durations and communication entries whose durations are left to the network model. Each accelerator issues its compute entries in order, as from a single stream. Ranks with identical durations and dependencies share an entry, so the plan size depends on the number of distinct rank behaviors, which arise only where the active experts do not divide evenly over the EP ranks.

An entry starts when its last predecessor ends. A communication entry registers its collective with the network model at its start time, and its end stays open until the network model reports it. When no further collective can be registered, the network model advances to the next completion, and the reported end times are substituted into the entries that depend on them. The network model therefore holds every collective that is in flight at a given time, e.g., the concurrent groups of one mesh axis, which share second-level links on the two-level fabrics. Simlette simulates these collectives together, so link contention and credit stalls between them lengthen their completion times, and the compute that waits for them starts later. Pricing each collective in isolation would miss both effects; the analytical model does so. Before the walk, the network model receives the traffic demand of Table 1, against which the OCS planner builds circuits (Section 3); a registered collective outside this demand is an error.

Without HOP-B, no communication overlaps with computation, so every collective lies on the critical path and a decode step is the sum of kernel durations, launch overheads, and collective completion times. The OCS saving per step is the reduction in collective completion time. This also matches the public implementations of Helix: TensorRT-LLM provides Helix parallelism, but its documented implementation does not yet include HOP-B’s batch-wise pipelining of attention computation and all-to-all communication, which NVIDIA lists as future work NVIDIA (2026a), and the Helix all-to-all backends recently added to vLLM vLLM Project (2026a) and SGLang SGLang Project (2026) do not describe such overlap. The following subsection Appendix B.5 shows that HOP-B would not shorten the evaluated decode steps.

B.5 Sensitivity to HOP-B

HOP-B Bhatia et al. (2025) splits the attention of a decode step into microbatches and overlaps the KV-parallel all-to-all of one microbatch with the attention computation of the next. The QKV projection, the FFN, and their collectives, i.e., the all-reduce after the output projection, the FFN all-reduce and expert all-gather, and the logit all-gather, still run once on the whole batch and are not overlapped. Figure 16 evaluates it for both models at batch 16 and 5M context, the largest batch and context of Section 6, which give HOP-B the most computation to overlap with.

Microbatching does not reduce the bytes of the all-to-all, but it issues the all-to-all once per microbatch in every layer. Its payload is divided among the calls, but each additional call adds the fixed latency of a collective, which dominates for the small payloads of decode (Table 1), so the communication time before overlap grows with the number of microbatches. HOP-B can hide this communication only behind attention, the all-to-all of the last microbatch stays exposed, and the decode step becomes shorter only if the hidden communication exceeds the added communication.

For GPT-OSS-5.3-like, it does not. A decode step computes for only 0.77 ms, half of its layers attend to a 128-token window, and HOP-B hides at most 0.34 ms of communication, while eight microbatches add 1.6 ms of communication on all-EPS. Against the step without HOP-B, the decode step grows by 6, 22, and 70 % on all-EPS with 2, 4, and 8 microbatches, and by 4, 11, and 29 % on all-OCS, whose collectives have the lowest latency per call. For Megatron 5T, attention over the 5M-token context dominates the 8.8 ms of computation per step and hides all added all-to-alls, but the exposed communication does not shrink: the all-to-all of the last microbatch takes as long as the single all-to-all without HOP-B, and the other collectives are not overlapped. The decode-step time is therefore unchanged on every fabric.

For the evaluated model-parallel configurations, microbatching with HOP-B does not improve decode-step time relative to a single microbatch. For GPT-OSS-5.3-like, the additional collective startup costs exceed the communication hidden through overlap. For Megatron 5T, the additional communication is almost entirely hidden, but the remaining exposed communication is unchanged. The single-microbatch configuration is therefore optimal or equivalent among the evaluated schedules, supporting its use in Section 6.

B.6 Searching the Parallelization Space

On NN accelerators, a Helix split (KVP, TPA, EP, TPE) satisfies KVP⋅TPA=EP⋅TPE=N\mathrm{KVP}\cdot\mathrm{TPA}=\mathrm{EP}\cdot\mathrm{TPE}=N, with power-of-two degrees, TPA dividing the number of KV heads, EP dividing the number of experts, and TPE dividing the expert width. At N=512N=512, this gives 72 splits for Megatron 5T and 45 for GPT-OSS-5.3-like.

For Figure 4, we choose a split per cell, i.e., per model, context (32K and 5M tokens), batch size (1, 2, 4, 8, and 16), and fabric. gxnet with the analytical network model of Section 5.4 times every split in every cell: 2160 points for Megatron 5T and 1350 for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, each simulated in under a second. The analytical model ignores contention and credit stalls (Section 5.4), so we re-simulate with Simlette every split whose analytical interactivity is within 7 % of the best split of its fabric in that cell, and report the best Simlette result per cell. This amounts to 758 points for Megatron 5T and 338 for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, with a median simulation time of about 10 minutes per point.

Appendix C Collective algorithms and time consumption in the Network Simulator

This appendix details how Simlette models collective communication on the evaluated network fabrics. It describes the simulator’s mapping stages, derives the analytical timing model, and explains the collective schedules and their consistency checks. It then presents simulation optimizations, hardware measurements used to parameterize latency, and the physical fabric configurations used in the evaluation.

C.1 Simlette Layers

Simlette separates the OCS-specific problem of mapping an ML workload to the physical network fabric into four layers, applied in the following order. The first is the topology: the physical host graph H=(V,E)H=(V,E) of devices, switches, and the ports that connect them, under the per-accelerator port budget LL introduced in Section 3.3. The second is worker allocation: the mapping of logical ranks onto this physical graph, i.e., the embedding of a logical overlay (Section 3.2) into the accelerators and links that will actually carry its traffic. The third is the collective, which supplies the schedule defined in Section 3.4: the ordered sequence of phases, the rank pairs and edges used at each phase, and the payload carried on each. This layer jointly searches over the collective and its logical topology, keeps the lowest-cost pair, and thereby determines the number of phases hih_{i}. The fourth is routing, which takes the chosen logical topology together with the physical topology and the allocation, and maps it onto concrete ports, paths, and circuit assignments. These four layers stay independent in the implementation.

C.2 Derivation of the Analytical Model

We compute the terms of Eq. 1 from the schedule of Section 3.4. Let bk,eb_{k,e} be the amount of data, in bytes, sent on logical edge ee during phase kk. All transfers of a phase start at the same time, and the phase ends when the transfer on the most loaded edge arrives. This transfer takes the latency λ\lambda of one hop, plus the time to put its data on the edge. The edge is made of pp parallel circuits of bandwidth RR each, expressed in bytes per second (400 Gb/s corresponds to R=50R=50 GB/s), so sending bk,eb_{k,e} takes bk,e/(p​R)b_{k,e}/(pR) and phase kk lasts λ+maxe⁡bk,e/(p​R)\lambda+\max_{e}b_{k,e}/(pR). Adding the hh phases gives Eq. 1, with the bottleneck volume

v=∑k=1hmaxe⁡bk,e,v=\sum_{k=1}^{h}\max_{e}b_{k,e}, (10)

i.e., the sum, over all phases, of the data carried by the most loaded edge of each phase. This assumes that phases do not overlap, and that no other collective uses the same links at the same time.

C.3 Collective Algorithms for Workload-static Switching

Each collective algorithm in Simlette computes hh, the schedule phase count, and vv, the bottleneck data volume, from its own phases, for a buffer size σ\sigma on a logical graph of NN ranks.

C.3.1 All-reduce schedules

Simlette implements the all-reduce schedules of Appendix A.3: the one-shot schedule, which reaches every rank within the diameter of the graph, and its data-volume-optimized variant (one-shot DVO), as well as the coset-factored and RS+AG schedules and their parallel variants, which exchange over one coset layer per phase (Tables 4 and 5).

Example: Analytical completion time of the all-reduce algorithms

Figure 17 shows the completion time of the all-reduce algorithms on N=512N=512 accelerators, from 1 KiB to 16 MiB. For small buffers the latency term h​λh\lambda is the largest, and the time depends mostly on the number of phases. For example, the two RS+AG algorithms take 18 phases, and their latency term is 18×0.52=9.4​μ18\times 0.52=9.4\,\mus. The other algorithms take only 9 phases, and their latency term is 9×0.52=4.7​μ9\times 0.52=4.7\,\mus.

For large buffers the bandwidth term v/(p​R)v/(pR) is the largest, and the algorithm that sends the least data is the fastest. Coset-factored sends the full buffer in each of its 9 phases. RS+AG sends only a part of the buffer in each phase, and about twice the buffer in total. RS+AG takes twice as many phases, but sends less data. The two curves cross at the buffer size where the extra phases of RS+AG cost as much time as the extra data of coset-factored. Below this size coset-factored is faster, and above it RS+AG is faster. Their parallel variants keep the same number of phases, but send 9 times less data on the most loaded link.

One-shot is the slowest at every size. At each phase, a rank sends to each neighbor every contribution it has received so far. This number grows from one phase to the next, and the same contributions cross the same links many times.

Topology-schedule interaction

Figure 18 shows the topology-schedule interaction at network level. The collective is a single all-reduce over N=64N=64 accelerators, with buffer sizes from 1 KiB to 16 MiB in powers of two. The schedule is coset-factored parallel, and the physical fabric is a single-level all-OCS with a radix of 13 ports per accelerator, of which L=12L=12 are used for circuits, and a bandwidth of R=400R=400 Gb/s per link.

C.3.2 All-to-all schedules

rr-Bruck (radix-rr Bruck all-to-all on a block fold, rr-Bruck takes h=ℓh=\ell phases on a fold of ℓ\ell layers. The all-to-all is uniform: every rank starts and ends with the same payload σ\sigma, so vv is the same for all ranks. rr-Bruck implements the Helix all-to-all of Table 1 in our evaluation.

C.4 Analytical Model against Simlette

The analytical model describes what we expect when nothing gets in the way, so without congestion Simlette should give the same results. To compare the two, we run single all-reduces on 32 accelerators connected by a single-level fabric with 400 Gb/s links, with buffer sizes from 1 KiB to 1 MiB and 8, 12, 16 or 24 ports per accelerator. All runs use persistent kernels, so a collective is complete when its last data arrives, as in the analytical model.

OCS.

Figure 19 uses the one-shot all-reduce, whose schedule never sends two flows on the same link at the same time, so there is no link contention. With an unlimited buffer, Simlette and the analytical model give the same results for all buffer sizes and radices, which shows that the simulator’s behavior is consistent with the model. If the buffer on each port is too small to keep a link busy for one hop, senders have to wait for credits, and Simlette is up to 1.9×1.9\times slower than the analytical model.

EPS: credit stalls.

Figure 20 uses the same one-shot all-reduce on EPS, again without link contention. With an unlimited buffer, Simlette and the analytical model agree within 5 % for small buffers and for buffers of 256 KiB and larger. For 16-64 KiB, however, Simlette is up to 29 % slower: a buffer this small yields per-port messages of only a few flits, which cannot be divided evenly across the links, so the busiest link carries more data than the analytical model assumes. With the buffer of every port reduced below what one hop needs to keep its link busy, senders wait for credits, which makes Simlette 1.6-1.7×\times slower than the analytical model. For example, with a 1 MiB buffer and 8 ports, the analytical model gives 82.1 μ\mus and Simlette 135.0 μ\mus: Simlette is 52.9 μ\mus slower, and its most delayed port spends 53.4 μ\mus waiting for credits.

EPS: link contention.

Figure 21 uses the two-shot all-reduce on EPS with an unlimited buffer, so there are no credit stalls. Two-shot consists of a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. In each phase, all accelerators send to the others in the same order, so they all target the same destination at the same time, and the switch port leading to that destination becomes congested. From 16 KiB onwards, Simlette is 1.5-2×\times slower than the analytical model, which counts the right amount of data on each link but cannot capture the time flows spend waiting for each other. The optimized mode of Simlette (Appendix C.5) gives almost the same results as the flit-by-flit mode, with less than 2 % difference.

C.5 Simlette Simulation Procedure Optimizations

Most of the latency along a hop is not paid at the point where it is decided in the simulation. When a switch or a scale-up port adds its share of delay, that delay is added to a timestamp carried on the message, while the operation handing the message to the next stage happens immediately, at the same simulated instant. Simulated time only moves forward at a few points: right before a port puts a message on the link, during serialization, and when a flit reaches its destination.

This deferred accounting matters because several flits are usually in flight at once: by the time a port is ready to send one, part of the delay it owes may already have elapsed while other flits were being processed elsewhere, so only the remaining gap, if any, still needs to be paid as a real wait. Simlette computes latency this way so that it always knows exactly how much of that gap is left to catch up, and never pays for the latency twice. The simulation stays exact even though every delay is resolved only when needed.

Simulating a message flit by flit means creating one event for every flit a device sends, rather than a single event for the whole message. At scale, this overhead itself costs real time to execute. A single all-reduce on a simple single-level topology with 256 accelerators and a 40 KiB buffer already takes about 14 minutes to simulate flit by flit. Larger buffers and more devices in the topology push this further, up to several hours. This is why Simlette also supports an optimized mode: the entire message is handed to the link in a single event, and the delay it would have accumulated flit by flit is charged at once on arrival. This way, only one event is created per message per transfer, instead of one event per flit per transfer. A flit is 640 bytes and a message can be tens of kilobytes, so flit-by-flit mode schedules dozens of events where the optimized mode schedules one; with the 40 KiB buffer of this experiment, a message spans up to 64 flits. As shown in Figure 21, both modes give almost the same completion times. Figure 22 compares the runtime of both modes as a function of accelerator count, on a fixed-radix topology (8 ports per accelerator) with a 40 KiB buffer, and shows the resulting speedup directly. From 32 to 256 accelerators, the optimized mode is consistently 77-9×9\times faster. For the 256-accelerator topology, this cuts runtime from 827 seconds down to 90 seconds.

Determinism

The simulation is currently fully deterministic: given the same topology, routing, and workload, every run produces the exact same completion time, with no randomness in link timing, arrivals, or failures. This makes results easy to reproduce and attribute to a single cause, but it does not capture the variability real hardware shows, so the completion times we report should be read as a best case rather than a distribution. This is particularly true for EPS based fabrics, where network-internal dynamics such as arbitration are well known to cause collective completion tail latencies.

C.6 Scale-up Latency Profiles

End-to-end measurements.

We characterize accelerator-to-accelerator communication latency using several ping-pong kernel implementations. Figure 23 illustrates the substantial implementation dependence of measured round-trip times. For model parameterization, we use the minimum observed latencies as an optimistic estimate of the hardware communication path.

Latency decomposition.

Figure 24 shows the latency component decomposition of network transactions on scale-up networks as modeled by the analytical network backend of gxnet and as used for the parametrization of our flit-based network simulator interfacing with gxnet. Note that this is not official NVIDIA data. The bare metal measurements carried out in Section 5.5 can only provide a limited number of known values to a set of equations that will then be underspecified. Specifically, allocating latency to the subcomponents “GPU MMU”, “TX”, “RX”, “SWITCH” (core switch latency) and “LINK TLB” is a matter of educated guesses. We believe that budgeting more latency into RX rather than TX sections is well justified by the FEC decode overhead alone.

Results for collective completion times in inference decode, especially for low-batch/high-interactivity cases, will be very susceptible to rebalancing spent latency between TX/RX stages and switch core. A lower switch pin-to-pin latency than the unloaded 300 ns assumed in this paper (64, Sec. 10.9.2) would translate into a smaller performance advantage for all-OCS based network fabrics - and this for two separate reasons: first, the latency difference between EPS and OCS switches as such would reduce. More importantly however, OCS fabrics rely on relaying information through the accelerator itself. A lower EPS pin-to-pin latency directly translates into higher accelerator ingress/egress latency because the absolute PE-to-PE latency must stay the same.

However, the opposite is of course also true: accelerators with very low ingress/egress latencies will emphasize the advantage of all-OCS fabrics. In light of recent industry trends to offload processing elements from collective communication tasks and introduce hardware based “collective acceleration engines” into the architectures (e.g., TPU 8i Google (2026)), the importance to lower switch pin-to-pin latencies in the network will grow in future systems.

Memory-hierarchy latency.

The accelerator-specific terms of the scale-up latency decomposition cover the path from the PE through the cache hierarchy to the scale-up port. We anchor them by replicating the pointer-chasing results of Table 3 in Luo et al. (2025) with the open-source microbenchmarks accompanying that paper, run on H100 and B300 (Table 8). On H100 we measure ≈\approx41 cycles (L1), ≈\approx29 cycles (shared memory) and ≈\approx276 cycles (L2), matching the published H800 values for shared memory and L2 and slightly exceeding the published L1 latency. On B300 the same binaries yield ≈\approx34, ≈\approx28.6 and ≈\approx277 cycles. Reading the GPU global timer from PTX instead of the cycle counter, and averaging over 30,000 samples, gives ≈\approx14.0 ns, ≈\approx16.7 ns and ≈\approx139.7 ns for shared memory, L1 and L2 respectively, without assuming an SM clock frequency. Two observations matter for the model: on-SM and L2-hit latency is effectively unchanged across two GPU generations, so it can be carried into future-accelerator scenarios with little risk; and L2, the deepest on-chip stage a remote access traverses, sits below 150 ns and is therefore a small fraction of the accelerator-to-accelerator path (Figure 24).

Scale-up latency parametrization variants

The latency profile break-down presented above has to work with a set of assumptions for the per-component latencies on the data path. In order to study sensitivity of our results to latency attribution variations, we choose three different attributions that either emphasize or de-emphasize the contribution of the EPS switch core (Table 9).

C.7 Physical Fabrics

We evaluate three scale-up fabric families as reference points for where optical circuits enter the accelerator-to-accelerator path. In all cases, each accelerator exposes LL links of bandwidth RR. We describe both packet- and circuit-switched fabrics by the paths available to collective schedules: hop count, per-hop latency, available bandwidth, and port consumption.

The all-EPS baseline represents a conventional electronic-packet-switched scale-up fabric. It provides flexible any-to-any connectivity, but traffic pays the latency of the electronic switching stages it traverses. The hybrid EPS/OCS fabric keeps local connectivity electronic while replacing the level-2 switches with deployment-time optical circuits, making it an incremental path from current EPS fabrics toward optical scale-up. The all-OCS fabric connects accelerator links directly to an optical circuit-switched fabric whose circuits are planned before serving starts and kept fixed throughout deployment.

The fabrics therefore differ in runtime routing flexibility and in how much electronic switching latency remains on accelerator-to-accelerator paths. In the all-OCS case, the full port budget LL can be assigned to the logical overlays induced by decode, either to reduce serialized communication phases, widen selected logical edges, or support multiple phase-specific overlays over the same accelerator set.

Concretely, each accelerator exposes L=36L=36 links of R=400R=400 Gb/s and all switching devices have a radix of 72, following NVL72-class systems. We instantiate a two-level electronic packet switch (EPS) based network (all-EPS), the same network with the devices on level 2 replaced by OCS (hybrid EPS/OCS), and a third topology in which all switching devices are OCS (all-OCS). In the all-EPS and hybrid fabrics, each level-1 switch uses 32 ports towards the accelerators and 8 towards level 2, i.e., a 4:1 oversubscription towards the second level, since a fully subscribed EPS spine with pluggable conversion exceeds a reasonable power envelope. The all-OCS fabric instead uses 32 ports in each direction and is thus non-blocking: its OCS devices require no E/O conversion and consume so little power per port (Appendix D.4) that the full uplink bandwidth still fits into a lower system power than either EPS-based fabric. Consequently, part of the all-OCS advantage for collective groups that span level 2 stems from this higher level-2 bandwidth rather than from the switching technology alone; the energy-efficiency results of Section 6 account for the full port count of each fabric.

Note that while the EPS based fabric uses all traits well-known to EPS based scale-up networks such as multi-path routing and packet spraying in accelerators and switches, the all-OCS fabric runs on the collective schedules presented in Section 3.4, which in turn make use of the topologies described in Section 3.2. The hybrid EPS/OCS fabric configures the OCS on the topmost level once at deployment, using the same planner to place workers such that bandwidth demand is balanced across the level-2 OCS devices, and otherwise relies on the same collective operations as implemented by current inference frameworks such as TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA (2026g), vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) or SGLang Zheng et al. (2024).

Appendix D Models and Accelerators

This appendix documents the model architectures, accelerator parameters, and power assumptions underlying the evaluation in Section 6, with model and accelerator specifications summarized in Tables 10 and 11. It also presents energy-efficiency results across the GPT-OSS family and examines the compute cost model against measured kernel durations, clarifying the assumptions and limitations of the projected accelerator results.

D.1 Models

Figures 26(a) and 26(b) show one decoder layer of each model. GPT-OSS-5.3-like is our extrapolation of the open-weight GPT-OSS-120B to the 5T scale. It keeps the GPT-OSS architecture recipe, namely interleaved sliding-window and full attention with a 128-token window and attention sinks, eight query heads per KV head, experts as wide as the hidden size with four active per token, and the 201,088-token vocabulary. It scales the hidden size from 2880 to 8192, the depth from 36 to 96 layers, the attention from 64 query and 8 KV heads to 128 and 16, and the expert count from 128 to 256.

The two models share their overall shape. Both are pre-norm decoders of about 5T parameters with a hidden size of 8192, in which grouped-query attention is followed by a mixture-of-experts FFN of 256 SwiGLU experts. Under Helix parallelism both issue the same five collectives at the same points of the layer, so the deployment-static structure of Table 1 is identical between them apart from the layer count. Because the hidden size is the same, the all-reduces and the expert all-gather also carry the same 4 KiB per token in both models.

The models differ above all in their attention, which decides how a decode step responds to context length.

  • •

    Interleaved sliding-window attention. GPT-OSS-5.3-like alternates between layers that attend only to the most recent 128 tokens and layers with full causal attention. The KV cache and attention time of a sliding-window layer do not depend on context length, so only 48 of its 96 layers read the whole context. Every one of Megatron’s 128 layers does. Removing the sliding window from GPT-OSS-5.3-like in gxnet doubles the part of its attention time that grows with context, from 0.39 to 0.77 ms per decode step between 32K and 5M context at batch 16.

  • •

    Narrow grouped-query attention. The full-attention layers of GPT-OSS-5.3-like keep 16 KV heads, eight query heads each. Megatron keeps 128 KV heads under 256 query heads, which also makes its attention 16,384 wide, twice the hidden size. Giving GPT-OSS-5.3-like Megatron’s 128 KV heads multiplies its context-dependent attention time by eight, to 3.1 ms in the same setting.

  • •

    KV cache. Together, the two points above give Megatron 1 MiB of KV cache per token of context against 48 KiB for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, a factor of 21. At 5M tokens one Megatron user occupies 5.2 TB of HBM and one GPT-OSS-5.3-like user 246 GB. This is what bounds the evaluated batch to 16 for Megatron on 512 accelerators, and it is why decode attention time grows much faster with batch and context for Megatron than for GPT-OSS-5.3-like (Section 6).

  • •

    Experts. Megatron’s experts are fine-grained (6144 wide, 0.75 of the hidden size) with eight active per token; those of GPT-OSS-5.3-like are as wide as the hidden size with four active. Megatron therefore activates 207 B parameters per token against 95 B.

  • •

    Vocabulary and details. GPT-OSS-5.3-like has a four times larger vocabulary, which only enlarges the LM head and the final logit all-gather. Its attention sinks and projection biases do not change the communication structure.

D.2 Energy Efficiency across the GPT-OSS Family

Figure 27 repeats the comparison of Figure 7 for three models of the GPT-OSS family: the open-weight GPT-OSS-120B on 8 accelerators at 32K context and batch 3413, GPT-OSS-1T-like on 64 accelerators at 128K context and batch 1024, and GPT-OSS-5.3-like on 512 accelerators at 5M context and batch 1. GPT-OSS-1T-like is an intermediate extrapolation of GPT-OSS-120B built like GPT-OSS-5.3-like, with a hidden size of 4608, 64 layers, 72 query and 8 KV heads, and 256 experts (Table 10). All-OCS fabrics improve throughput per unit energy by 32 %, 67 % and 119 %, respectively. For GPT-OSS-120B, whose deployment spans only eight accelerators, interactivity is practically unchanged (−1-1 %), so the gain stems from system power alone; for GPT-OSS-1T-like, interactivity improves by 26 %, and for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, whose decode step is dominated by communication (Figure 5), by 65 %.

D.3 Accelerators

RX00 is a projected accelerator modeled on announced Rubin figures (as announced at GTC in March 2026 NVIDIA (2026c)), so its kernel durations cannot be measured. Its parameters in Table 11 are peak throughput and bandwidth; the efficiency functions of Appendix B.3 are a step approximation of curves measured on H100, which we use unchanged for B200 and RX00.

The cost model is a roofline with size-dependent efficiencies and no fixed cost per kernel. Operators between two collectives form one execution window that pays a single in-graph launch overhead, which assumes they run back to back as in a persistent kernel Cheng et al. (2025). The model therefore gives a lower bound on compute time rather than a prediction of a particular kernel implementation.

We choose a roofline deliberately. Predicting kernel durations more precisely requires either profiling operators on the target accelerator, as in Vidur Agrawal et al. (2024a), or models fitted to measurements of existing kernels, such as PipeWeave Zhang et al. (2026). The first is impossible for an unreleased accelerator. The second generalizes to held-out GPUs of architectures seen in training, e.g., from H20 and H800 to H100 and H200, but has not been shown to carry over to a new architecture generation, and reports no separate error for the small batch sizes of decode, where durations depend on kernel setup, tiling, and occupancy rather than on FLOPs and bytes. Such models can be more accurate on the hardware they were fitted to, but their error on a new architecture has neither a known size nor a known sign. The error of a roofline has a known sign: it underestimates.

We compared the model with Nsight Systems traces of GPT-OSS-120B decode on four B200 with tensor parallelism and CUDA-graph replay, at batch sizes 1 to 16. The decode kernels there read a few to a few tens of MB per accelerator and reach 12 to 53 % of the peak HBM bandwidth, below the efficiencies of Appendix B.3, so the H100 curves remain optimistic one generation later. Even under CUDA-graph replay, no kernel finishes in less than about 3 μ\mus. These decode kernels therefore take 1.4 to 5 times as long as their roofline estimate, and more for the smallest ones. A persistent-kernel implementation avoids part of this per-kernel cost, which is the execution our fused windows assume.

Since the model underestimates compute time, the share of communication in a decode step, and with it the relative OCS gain of Section 6, is an upper estimate, while the absolute reduction of collective completion time per step does not depend on the compute model. For existing accelerators, gxnet can replace the roofline estimate of any operator with a measured kernel duration without changing the graph or the sharding.

D.4 Power Model

Our power models are based on publicly available data. In conjunction with the topologies described in Appendix C.7, we always assume that moving between scale-up network levels 1 and 2 requires optical cabling (due to rack-to-rack distance) and that all-OCS based topologies make use of CPO at the accelerator. The power figures we use for the system components are given in Table 12, together with their origin wherever applicable.

Table 12 lists the power figures used by the model. All values are thermal-design (maximum) figures, so the model gives an upper bound on power independent of traffic. Per-XPU power is not the accelerator TDP. We take the designed rack power of an NVL72-class system NVIDIA (), subtract the scale-up switch trays, and divide by the 72 accelerators. The resulting figure therefore includes each XPU’s share of host CPU, NICs, DPU, fans and voltage-regulation losses.

No public figure exists for the GB200/GB300 switch tray, so we assume 1.7 kW1.7\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{W}. We cross-check this value by scaling the published power of a 51.2 Tb/s51.2\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s} scale-up Ethernet switch ASIC (800 W800\text{\,}\mathrm{W} Broadcom (2025)) to the two 28.8 Tb/s28.8\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s} switch ASICs per tray SemiAnalysis (). We then apply the system-to-ASIC overhead observed for Tomahawk 5 (913 W913\text{\,}\mathrm{W} system without optics IP Infusion () versus about 500 W500\text{\,}\mathrm{W} ASIC TechInsights ()). This yields about 1.64 kW1.64\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{W}, within 4 % of our assumption.

No rack power has been published for Vera Rubin NVL72. We use the 220 kW220\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{W} Max-P estimate of SemiAnalysis (), which agrees with the 227 kW227\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{W} per-rack cooling sizing of an OEM reference design Supermicro (). The rack’s power shelves (4×110 kW4\times$110\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{W}$, N+1) define a provisioning ceiling, not a TDP. The Rubin tray holds four switch ASICs instead of two NVIDIA (). Each ASIC keeps the per-ASIC bandwidth of 28.8 Tb/s28.8\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s} SemiAnalysis (), so we double the tray power. Per 400 G400\text{\,}\mathrm{G}-equivalent port, the scale-up switching power is therefore the same as for GB200.

EPS ports at 800 G800\text{\,}\mathrm{G} and 1.6 T1.6\text{\,}\mathrm{T} are extrapolated from the 400 G400\text{\,}\mathrm{G} anchor assuming a 35 % energy-per-bit reduction per doubling of port rate. This is the reduction observed between the 25.6 and 51.2 Tb/s51.2\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s} generations of switch systems measured on the same basis (typical power, excluding optics) Arista Networks (); Arista Networks ().

OCS figures are internal projections for a switch whose ports each use two unidirectional fibers. The power per port is 1.5 W1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{W} at 400 G400\text{\,}\mathrm{G}.

Every switching device, EPS or OCS, is evaluated with all of its physical ports, whether a port is used or not. On the level-1 switches of the EPS-based fabrics, which use 40 of their 72 ports, this is conservative, but the per-port figure amortizes device-level power, such as that of the switch ASIC core, which does not scale down with unused ports.

Optical links attach either through one pluggable transceiver per port or through co-packaged optics (CPO). For CPO we use the energy per bit published for switch-side optical engines, including the external laser source, and multiply by the unidirectional rate. We assume the same CPO energy per bit when an accelerator attaches directly to the level-1 OCS switches.

Appendix E Sensitivity Analysis

This appendix examines the sensitivity of the evaluation results to network bandwidth, accelerator radix, switch and endpoint latency, and communication precision. These analyses assess how the relative performance and energy efficiency of the evaluated fabrics depend on the baseline configuration and modeling assumptions.

Figure 28 varies one fabric or accelerator parameter at a time for GPT-OSS-5.3-like at batch 1 and 5M context, the latency-bound regime of Section 6. The parallelization is re-optimized for every point, and all four sweeps share the baseline of Section 6, with a 64.8 % interactivity and a 118.7 % energy-efficiency advantage of all-OCS over all-EPS. Since energy efficiency is throughput per system power, the energy advantage is the interactivity advantage multiplied by the ratio of all-EPS system power to that of the respective fabric, which is 1.33 for all-OCS at the baseline.

Per-port bandwidth.

At batch 1, the interactivity advantage of all-OCS is nearly insensitive to bandwidth, staying between 62.8 % and 65.2 % between 400 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s. Since the all-EPS baseline is oversubscribed towards its second level, it carries a bandwidth-bound component that shrinks with per-port bandwidth, whereas the non-blocking all-OCS fabric has little to gain. The energy advantage of all-OCS nevertheless grows from 119 % to 161 %, as the power ratio rises from 1.33 to 1.60: per rate doubling, EPS port power grows by 30 % and pluggable power almost doubles, while OCS port power grows by only 10 % and the energy per bit of CPO decreases (Appendix D.4). The hybrid fabric does not benefit, since it retains electronic level-1 switches and pluggables on every link between the two levels.

Accelerator radix.

Co-packaged optics allow the accelerator radix to grow. For inference decode, additional ports pay off substantially at first: the interactivity advantage of all-OCS rises from 65 % at 36 ports to 88 % at 48 ports and 100 % at 64 ports, but then saturates at 104 % and 103 % for 96 and 128 ports. Along the way, the planner changes the parallelization of all-OCS: it keeps the baseline split up to 48 ports (32/16/2/256 in KVP/TPA/EP/TPE), spreads the FFN over a single tensor-parallel group of all 512 accelerators (32/16/1/512) at 64 and 128 ports, and uses 32/16/8/64 at 96 ports, so additional ports buy freedom of parallelization as much as speed. The saturation follows from the schedulable frontier of Appendix A.2: phase counts drop in discrete steps, each further step costs considerably more ports than the previous one, e.g., two phases on an axis of 64 accelerators cost 14 ports and one phase 63, and ports between two steps buy no phase reduction. At a fixed system size, more accelerator radix therefore affords larger scale-up domains, or links for network-attached memory, rather than higher interactivity directly. In energy efficiency, however, the advantage of all-OCS keeps growing to 293 %, as the power ratio rises from 1.33 to 1.94 with every port added to the packet-switched fabric.

Switch latency attribution.

Our measurements (Section 5.5) cannot separate accelerator from switch latency, and the unloaded 300 ns pin-to-pin latency of the UALink specification Ultra Accelerator Link Consortium (2025) may be exceeded under load. We therefore keep the 810 ns per switch hop of Table 9 constant and shift latency between accelerator and switch core. Since the all-OCS path bypasses the switch core, every nanosecond moved into the switch shortens it: the interactivity advantage grows from 30 % to 65 % and 160 % for switch core latencies of 100, 200, and 400 ns, at a constant power ratio of 1.33. The results are thus highly sensitive to where latency is spent, which explains the effort of recent architectures to keep latency-critical traffic within a single switch level: Jalapeño bifurcates its links into separate single-level domains for tensor and expert parallelism Ho et al. (2026), a design-time counterpart of the stacked-link allocation of Appendix A.6.

Accelerator latency.

Reducing accelerator egress and ingress latency benefits both fabrics, but all-OCS considerably more, since its per-hop latency consists almost entirely of accelerator latency: its interactivity advantage changes by about 9 to 12 percentage points per 100 ns, from 88 % at 300 ns to 55 % at 600 ns. The hybrid fabric gains almost nothing, as it runs the same packet-switched collective schedules over the same electronic level-1 paths as all-EPS. Collective acceleration engines Google (2026) that shorten the accelerator-side path therefore directly increase the advantage of workload-static OCS, and so does lighter forward error correction: an EPS switch terminates FEC at every hop, whereas a passive optical path is terminated once at its endpoints. Scale-Up Ethernet names RS-272 as a candidate to reduce receive latency (Broadcom Inc., , Sec. 3.5.4), with link-level retransmission as the hardware-based safety net for residual errors.

Communication precision.

Our baseline models activation communication in FP4, consistent with the assumed activation storage precision (Appendix B.1). This is a forward-looking assumption: many serving collectives still communicate in BF16, including the default MoE combine paths in DeepEP DeepSeek-AI (2026) and TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA (2026d). However, lower-precision transport is already supported for MoE dispatch (FP8/NVFP4) and optionally for combine (NVFP4)  DeepSeek-AI (2026); NVIDIA (2025); NVIDIA (2026d).

To assess sensitivity to communication precision, we repeat the evaluation of Figure 4 using BF16 activation transfers, quadrupling the bytes per activation element relative to FP4, while Helix softmax statistics are communicated in FP32. For each precision, we independently repeat the full parallelization search of Appendix B.6, selecting the best-performing configuration for each workload and fabric. We account for the resulting communication volumes but do not model precision-conversion overheads or numerical accuracy effects.

All-OCS continues to outperform all-EPS in every configuration, with an interactivity advantage of 9.6–75.7 %, compared with 7.3–81.6 % under FP4. Up to batch size 8, the advantage generally decreases by up to 16 percentage points. At batch size 16, it instead increases by 1–3 points, consistent with additional bandwidth pressure on the oversubscribed EPS fabric. The hybrid fabric changes by at most 3 points, except for Megatron 5T at 32K context and batch size 16, where its advantage decreases from 12.5 to 5.7 %.

Thus, the relative benefits depend on communication precision, but the conclusions of Section 6 remain unchanged. The HOP-B findings (Appendix B.5) are also robust: repeated all-to-all startup costs continue to outweigh overlap savings for GPT-OSS-5.3-like, whose decode-step time under BF16 increases by 58 % on all-EPS and 24 % on all-OCS with eight microbatches.
